The Brand New IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card

Earn up to $4,300 in travel value when you spend $120,000 in your first 4 months as a cardholder

As High As 175,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

The  is one of the most recognizable premium travel rewards cards on the market, offering everything from airport lounge access and hotel elite status to a long list of travel and lifestyle statement credits.

But with an $895 annual fee (see rates and fees), it's also a significant investment.

The Amex Platinum offers plenty of opportunities to offset that cost, especially if you travel frequently and can take advantage of its statement credits. However, many of its benefits come with restrictions, and getting the full value requires some effort.

So, who can actually get enough value from the Amex Platinum to justify its annual fee? Let's take a closer look at who should — and shouldn't — consider adding this card to their wallet.

For frequent travelers, airport lounge access is one of the biggest reasons to consider the .

The card offers access to one of the most extensive airport lounge networks available through a credit card, making it especially valuable if you spend a lot of time in airports.

Cardmembers can access American Express Centurion Lounges, receive a Priority Pass Select membership (enrollment required) and visit Delta Sky Clubs when flying on eligible same-day Delta flights. Delta Sky Club access is limited to 10 visits per year unless you spend $75,000 on eligible purchases in a calendar year to unlock unlimited visits. Access is subject to eligibility requirements.

Amex also operates Centurion Lounges at more than 20 airports, so the benefit can be particularly valuable if you live near or frequently connect through an airport with one.

If you travel frequently and would otherwise pay for lounge access, the Platinum could help you save money while making your time at the airport more comfortable. And when combined with the card's other travel benefits and statement credits, lounge access can help make the $895 annual fee easier to justify.

While the is best known for its premium travel benefits, it also offers a growing list of lifestyle statement credits that can help offset its $895 annual fee.

For example, cardmembers can receive up to $400 in Resy statement credits each calendar year (distributed as up to $100 per quarter) at eligible U.S. Resy restaurants* and up to $300 in Lululemon statement credits* (up to $75 quarterly) at U.S. stores (excluding outlets) and online.

The card also offers up to $300 annually in digital entertainment statement credits* (up to $25 monthly) for eligible subscriptions, along with up to $120 annually toward an Uber One membership to fully cover an auto-renewing $96 annual or $9.99 monthly membership*.

If you're already spending money on dining, shopping and entertainment in these categories, the credits can provide meaningful value without requiring you to change your spending habits.

However, many of these benefits are divided into monthly or quarterly credits, so you'll need to keep track of when to use them. The Platinum is a particularly good fit for someone who doesn't mind managing these benefits and can consistently take advantage of them year-round.

Related: How to maximize benefits with the American Express Platinum

The Amex Platinum can also be a valuable addition to your wallet if you regularly stay at Hilton, Marriott or luxury hotels.

Cardmembers receive complimentary Hilton Honors Gold and Marriott Bonvoy Gold Elite status, which can provide benefits such as bonus points on stays and potential room upgrades. You'll also receive Leaders Club Sterling status with The Leading Hotels of the World, a collection of independent luxury hotels. Enrollment is required for select benefits.

Beyond elite status, one of the Platinum's most valuable hotel-related perks is its up to $600 annual lodging statement credit (up to $300 semiannually).

Cardmembers can receive up to $300 in statement credits every six months on eligible prepaid bookings through American Express Travel®, including stays at Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection properties, as well as select Airbnb Luxe stays.

The Hotel Collection and Airbnb Luxe require a minimum two-night stay, and beginning Jan. 1, 2027, Fine Hotels + Resorts bookings will also require at least two nights to qualify for the lodging credit.

Fine Hotels + Resorts bookings also come with valuable benefits, including daily breakfast for two, guaranteed 4 p.m. late checkout, room upgrades when available and a property credit valued at $100.

If you regularly book these types of stays, the lodging credit and additional perks can go a long way toward offsetting the card's annual fee. Just be sure to compare prices with booking directly, since rates through Amex Travel aren't always the lowest.

Related: How to maximize the Amex Platinum hotel statement credit

Chase's unofficial 5/24 rule generally makes applicants ineligible for many Chase cards if they've opened five or more personal credit cards across issuers within the past 24 months.

Travelers who are still eligible for Chase cards may want to prioritize products such as the (see rates and fees) or (see rates and fees) before exceeding that threshold.

If you've already built a collection of Chase rewards cards, the Amex Platinum could be worth considering as your next premium travel card.

The card also earns Membership Rewards points, giving you access to a separate collection of airline and hotel transfer partners that can complement an existing Chase Ultimate Rewards strategy.

Many people just starting in the points world underestimate the stringency of Chase’s 5/24 rule. If you're just getting started with travel rewards and remain under Chase's 5/24 threshold, you may want to think carefully before applying for the Amex Platinum.

Opening the card could count toward your 5/24 total and potentially limit your eligibility for Chase cards in the future. That could mean missing out on valuable welcome offers or benefits from cards you planned to open later.

However, once you get over 5/24, it may be hard to get back under, and there’s a massive opportunity cost in doing so. Having a plan and sticking to it will serve you well in the long term.

Of course, that doesn't mean everyone under 5/24 should avoid the Platinum. If its benefits are a particularly good fit for your travel habits, it may still make sense.

The provides 5 Membership Rewards points per dollar spent on flights booked directly with airlines or with American Express Travel (on up to $500,000 of spending each calendar year, then 1 point per dollar spent).

A card like the or (see rates and fees) may be a better fit because their broader travel earning categories can include eligible third-party airfare bookings.

The offers a long list of statement credits, but that doesn't necessarily mean every cardholder will get enough value from them to justify the $895 annual fee.

Following the card's 2025 refresh, several of its benefits are geared toward specific lifestyle purchases, including dining at Resy restaurants, shopping at Lululemon and purchasing an Oura Ring. (Cardmembers receive up to a $200 Oura Ring statement credit each calendar year. This statement credit applies to ring purchases only and doesn't cover subscriptions. Enrollment is required.)

Many of these credits also come with restrictions. For example, the Resy and Lululemon credits are distributed quarterly, meaning you'll need to use them throughout the year rather than all at once.

If you don't already spend money with these merchants, or you don't want to keep track of multiple credits and enrollment requirements, the Platinum may not be the best fit.

Before applying, carefully consider just how much these credits are worth to you; if they provide little to no value, another Amex card might be a better fit.

Related: 4 different flavors of Amex Platinum — which one is right for you?

Business owners with substantial expenses may find that is a better fit than the personal Platinum.

Although both cards carry an $895 annual fee (see rates and fees), their earning rates and statement credits differ in ways that could make one more valuable than the other.

For example, the Business Platinum earns 2 points per dollar spent on eligible purchases in select business categories and on purchases of $5,000 or more, on up to $2 million in combined eligible purchases per calendar year, then 1 point per dollar.

The Business Platinum also provides up to $1,150 in statement credits per calendar year for U.S. Dell purchases: up to $150 each calendar year and an additional $1,000 statement credit after spending $5,000 on Dell purchases with the same card each calendar year (enrollment required).

You can also access the Pay with Points redemption option on the Business Platinum card, which gets you a 35% bonus for eligible flights with your selected airline using your Amex points (up to 1 million points back per calendar year). This is notably not available on the personal Amex Platinum.

These business-focused benefits may be more useful for someone with significant company expenses, while the personal Platinum may be a better fit for travelers who can maximize its lifestyle credits.

New cardmembers can find out their offer and may be eligible for as high as 175,000 bonus points after spending $12,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, that bonus could be worth up to $3,500, which is nearly four times the card's $895 annual fee.

While this is the card's standard welcome offer, now could still be a good time to apply if you're eligible for an offer you're happy with and can comfortably meet the spending requirement without making unnecessary purchases.

Just make sure you'll also get enough value from the card's ongoing benefits to justify its annual fee beyond the first year.

Related: The best time to apply for Amex cards based on offer history

The offers an impressive lineup of premium travel benefits and statement credits, but its $895 annual fee means it won't make sense for everyone.

For frequent travelers who value airport lounge access and luxury hotel perks, and can consistently use the card's lifestyle credits, there's plenty of potential to get more value than the annual fee.

On the other hand, travelers who prefer straightforward rewards or don't regularly use the card's benefits may find better value with a lower-annual-fee option.

Ultimately, the Platinum is worth considering if its benefits fit your existing spending and travel habits — not because of the total advertised value of its credits.

#6198. JetBlue Cancels All Flights On 35 Routes: See Full List Now

JetBlue has removed a considerable 35 routes from its network, of which 22 are domestic and 13 are international. They all operated at some point in the first ten months of 2026, but no flights are scheduled in the future.

In winter 2026/2027, JetBlue's schedule submission to Cirium Diio data shows an average of 919 daily departures (double for total movements). Compared to the prior winter, 7% more activity is scheduled. By far the main winner is Fort Lauderdale, with departures up by a staggering 58%, influenced by the end of Spirit. In contrast, Newark flights are down by 32%.

Analyzing the evolving carrier's entire network identified that the following markets no longer exist. The examined period only includes January to October 2026, with any routes that will end in November 2026 or thereafter not mentioned. They'll be explored separately another time.

No JetBlue Flights Now Exist On These Routes

New York JFK to Ponce (in the US territory of Puerto Rico)

Boston to Dallas/Fort Worth, Bozeman to Fort Lauderdale (limited flights for spring break), Denver to Fort Lauderdale (limited flights for spring break), New York JFK to Tampa, Reno to Fort Lauderdale (limited flights for spring break), Salt Lake City to Fort Lauderdale (limited flights for spring break)

Portland to Fort Lauderdale (limited flights for spring break), Providence to Fort Myers

Manchester to Fort Lauderdale, Manchester to Fort Myers

Newark to Fort Myers, Newark to Las Vegas

Hartford to Tampa, Manchester to Orlando, Newark to Tampa

Boston to Daytona Beach, New York JFK to Daytona Beach, New York JFK to Vero Beach

Newark to Los Angeles, New York JFK to Chicago O'Hare, New York JFK to Nashville

Despite the big overall growth at Fort Lauderdale, the South Florida airport has seen the most eliminated domestic routes. However, this is primarily because most only operated very briefly for spring break. The cuts included Reno, from which no flights to Fort Lauderdale (or Florida generally) previously existed. Given the US Department of Transportation (DOT) shows a load factor of 60.1%, it is hardly surprising that JetBlue isn't returning.

As is usually the case, some of the eliminated markets related directly to JetBlue pulling out of certain cities entirely. The last flights to Manchester, New Hampshire, existed in July 2026, while the airline's final service to Daytona Beach ended two months later. JetBlue only returned to the Florida city in December 2025, having previously flown there until January 2019.

All the following markets had nonstop flights with JetBlue at some point between January and October this year, but no service is now scheduled. The cuts contribute to JetBlue's overall international flights falling by 2% this winter. In contrast, the carrier's domestic activity has risen by 11% compared to last winter. JetBlue has now pulled out of Antigua, Belize City, Bonaire, and Tulum.

No JetBlue Flights Now Exist On These Routes

New York JFK to Belize City, New York JFK to Guatemala City, New York JFK to San Pedro Sula

Fort Lauderdale to Grand Cayman, Tampa to Punta Cana (Breeze entered this market in March this year)

Newark to Antigua, Newark to Cancun, Newark to Punta Cana, Newark to Santo Domingo, Orlando to San Jose

Like the experience of other airlines, service to the Mexican tourist gateway of Tulum did not last long. JetBlue flew there for less than two years, running between June 2024 and March 2026. Only New York JFK was served. DOT data shows that 91,226 round-trip passengers were carried, but just 70.4% of seats were filled. However, at least the airline tried, with the aircraft redeployed to where it may perform better.

Only half of the seats were filled. Find out more here!

DOT data provides passenger traffic and load factor information. This source was used to explore JetBlue's entire network in the 12 months to July 2026. Six routes met the criteria of having at least 5,000 round-trip passengers but a load factor not exceeding 50.0%.

They are Boston to Martha's Vineyard (9,333 passengers; 45.8%), Boston to Steamboat Springs (6,529 passengers; 49.8%), Boston to Presque Isle (42,119 passengers; 43.5%), Fort Lauderdale to Orlando (26,664 passengers; 48.3%), New York JFK to Hartford (53,383 passengers; 46.5%), and New York JFK to Providence (47,073 passengers; 41.1%).

The very short hops from the Big Apple are arguably for slot-sitting purposes, although connectivity via JFK will be important. Like the others, especially those with decent traffic, they may also all play an important network role even if they do not make a profit by themselves. But given how empty they are, for how long will they realistically last?

#6197. United Airlines Bans “AI Agents,” Claims It’s To “Protect Customers”

United Airlines has just banned travelers from using “AI Agents” to book or service tickets (thanks to TravelinWilly for flagging this). That’s an interesting stance for United, easily the country’s most tech savvy airline, to take. So what’s actually going on here?

United Airlines has today updated its contract of carriage, which are the terms that passengers have to agree to when they book a ticket. In the section about prohibited practices at the airline, the carrier added the following:

The use of AI Agents to make, modify or service a Ticket, and/or to purchase any service or product.

The “AI Agents” term is defined by United as follows:

AI Agent means any software or service, including but not limited to an AI assistant, AI agent or AI-enabled browser that takes autonomous or semi-autonomous action, whether or not Passenger or another individual supervises or approves its actions, to discover, search for, book, purchase, ticket, service or manage any product or service offered by or through United, including flights, seats, upgrades, ancillary products and partner products, on behalf of or at the instruction of Passenger or other individual. AI Agents include but are not limited to: (i) AI assistants built into social media, messaging, search or other consumer platforms; (ii) AI-enabled browsers and standalone AI agents; and (iii) any third-party AI assistant that accesses United through a tool, application or connection provided by a travel agency or other intermediary.

United even put out a press release about this change, claiming that it’s making the change to “protect” customers. Here’s part of the explanation:

Sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles. Plus, these automated AI actions have the potential to violate FAA and DOT regulations – as an example, flight check-in requires human acknowledgment that bags do not contain banned substances like explosives.

United claims it’s taking steps to restrict this kind of access, both directly within its digital platforms, and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators, to prohibit use by unauthorized, third party personal AI agents or assistants.

It goes without saying that use of AI is becoming exponentially more popular in recent times, and is a force to be reckoned with. It’s anyone’s guess just how far it goes, in terms of how much the average person uses it in their everyday life.

There are certainly aspects of AI that are incredibly annoying, whether you look at it as an individual or a business. Admittedly I’m biased, but I’m so tired of feeling like half of what I’m reading online (whether on social media or websites) is written by a computer and not a human. It even extends to things like TripAdvisor reviews.

It’s also frustrating how many people write 30 paragraph emails nowadays, which are clearly 90% AI. I don’t really understand how that makes anyone’s life better. As far as I’m concerned, just give me the bullet points you fed your AI buddy, and we’ll all be better off for it. Anyway, rant over, back to United…

I suspect United’s real motive here is that it doesn’t want AI automatically being able to track and reprice flights (and then issue vouchers for passengers), or being able to too closely compare overall value on different airlines. For that matter, it probably just doesn’t want a third party getting that much data on the airline, not to mention that all of this can take a considerable toll on servers, if this scales.

But here’s what I find most interesting — the way this rule is written strikes me as being incredibly broad, no? Not to repeat the quote again, but this is the part I’m referencing, in particular:

AI Agent means any software or service, including but not limited to an AI assistant, AI agent or AI-enabled browser that takes autonomous or semi-autonomous action, whether or not Passenger or another individual supervises or approves its actions, to discover, search for, book, purchase, ticket, service or manage any product or service offered by or through United, including flights, seats, upgrades, ancillary products and partner products, on behalf of or at the instruction of Passenger or other individual.

Any software that automatically “discovers” or searches for any product or service offered by United would include all award search tools (along with all kinds of other businesses), no? Is that actually the intent here, or does United just plan to selectively enforce rules? We did see Air Canada engage in a battle over this a few years back, so is United planning something similar?

United Airlines has today updated its rules to ban “AI Agents,” and the airline even put out a press release about it. The company claims it’s making this change to protect customers and their accounts, as AI bots could have unintended consequences.

Many people are understandably skeptical of that explanation, as I imagine the airline also wants to ban these kinds of things to help people reprice tickets, get better fares, etc. For that matter, based on how broadly the definition is written, it seems that even things like award search engines would be banned.

On one hand, it's easy to look at United's motive here. They don't want to lose revenue, and AI / MCP capabilities can easily get around some of the scraping restrictions that they've built over the last decade. But a level deeper, we're also seeing the same thing in finance. And retail. Heck, AI is even eating Google's core business. There's probably a good degree of fear from every industry that something big is coming and rather than learn to adapt, take risks and aim to thrive, they do what America does best: ban it and tell you it's for security.

The future is here. I had 1 of my AI agents (Insight) monitoring hotel reservations. It found cheaper rates on the same dates for 2 existing reservations & asked if I would like it to book the new reservation & cancel the old. I agreed. A hotel in London is > $200 cheaper. One in Perth $10 cheaper (ha ha). But since there was little time cost to me to let it rebook the Perth reservation, I said go ahead. But I gave permission first & reviewed the new reservations & cancellations afterward.

Personally, I am glad they imposed this ban. Whatever their reason is I don't care. As a iT security guy, allowing an agent to interface with booking opens up soooooo many security breach potentials and nearly impossible to explain it to a exec or govt official in a way they would understand. To the point the regulators would just dismiss what they don't understand as fear mongering. Companies just cannot randomly deloy AI features. To date none of them including big tech are treating ai security with any seriousness. The only security right now is good enough for optics and counting on the public not understanding how this stuff works. All the scamming attempts we get now will be magnify by 1000x and the speed of the scale will increase dramatically. Binance getting hacked and losing $6B should be a big big warning given that they have much more security than an airline. I am tell you unequivocally airline data security is laughable. United airline for example, their IT don't even know what 2 FA actually is. Their website have some lame security and they call it 2FA not even realizing what they implemented actually made their security worse. These ceos think AI is magic. They're going to get a very hard lesson on AI and AI security. The one blessing I have is that because I churn credit cards so often I'm not concern about cc data breaches or stolen card #. But everything else, we're in for some pain.

I think this is likely a combination of pricing data protection (there are sites today that have a lot of access but there are limits to how it can be leveraged individually, whereas you could have your own agent do data scrapes specific to flights you want to book), and getting ahead of the potential for thousands of individual agents scraping airline websites and either causing stability issues or running up their hosting costs. They also want to protect their own ability to create their own agents that have unique access to their data (and potentially charging for that). Amazon has done the same thing - and went as far as to limit the descriptions and details they provide in order emails now so Google can't scrape the data from Gmail accounts.

It's pretty clear that when an AI agent books a ticket for the user, United is not liable for mistake. What's more interesting, though, is if there's a third party service like cheapflights.ai or something that the user can pay to book them a good flight. If the website screws up, is the user or cheapflights.ai liable? More abstractly, in an agentic SaaS scenario, does the agent owner or the agent operator bear liability?

#6196. LGBTQ representation on TV fell during 2025-26 season, GLAAD says

#6195. Singapore Airlines Reconsiders New Business Class Seat Design After Backlash

Last week, Singapore Airlines unveiled all-new cabins, with the most exciting developments being a new first class and new business class. The new cabins look great (nothing revolutionary, but a huge improvement), with one exception — the new business class seat colors. Not only do they look cheap, but they just seem completely mismatched to the rest of the cabin.

While the airline vehemently defended the color choices for several days, it seems that they’re at least now reconsidering it, though it remains to be seen if it’s too late to make a change…

On Wednesday, November 11, 2026, Singapore Airlines CEO Goh Choon Phong had a town hall with employees, as reported by The Business Times. During this, he was asked about the negative feedback the airline has received about the new business class seat design.

In response to this, he reportedly said “we’ll look at it, we’ll see what’s feasible.” So that signals some willingness to make changes, though admittedly with how far out seats are ordered, that’s not necessarily so straightforward, so I wouldn’t count on anything happening. He did, however, emphasize that customers will come to like the seats after experiencing its comforts for themselves.

At the town hall, Singapore Airlines Chief Commercial Officer Lee Lik Hsin said this was a good learning point for the airline, but indicated that he hopes customers will mind the colors less after experiencing the seats. He also reportedly said “I suppose, you know, it’s the 80-20 rule, you can’t please them all.”

At the time of launch, Singapore Airlines VP of Product Experience, Ong Wah Li, explained the new design was in response to customer feedback, and described it as “modern, fresh, yet elegant and refined, that’s suited to business travel.”

BMW Designworks was behind the design of the cabin, and CEO Julia de Bono defended the color choices at the launch event, describing them as “more refreshing and more progressive.” As she viewed it, “what I see when I look at it, it’s definitely like a nice suit, with the white and the metal really popping out, you know, it’s more like a suit with a sneaker, so a bit more modern and fresh.”

To state the obvious, the trim and finishes on a new business class seat are hardly the most pressing issues facing the world. However, Singapore Airlines prides itself in being perhaps the most detail oriented airline in the world, because management has an obsessive attention to even the smallest things.

So I can’t help but be a bit confused by all of this:

It also just feels to me like the mandate for the design of this product was off, as shared by the CEO of BMW Designworks. Premium travel demand is through the roof, and a lot of people in premium cabins aren’t traveling for business. For that matter, these cabins will be operating the world’s longest flights, so this isn’t a case of a business traveler hopping on a plane in a suit, and going straight to a meeting (at least that doesn’t make up a meaningful percentage of the traffic here).

Is “suit with a sneaker” really the vibe you want to go for with a new business class product that’s on an airline that’s known for its incredible warmth? It’s almost like the airline views warmth and modernity as being at odds with one another, which I don’t at all agree with.

For example, reader Sam asked AI to take the new seat, but preserve the old color concept, and below is what it spit out.

That looks so much more on brand for Singapore Airlines than what the airline actually arrived at.

I would’ve loved to be a fly on the wall when this design was finalized. Was everyone immediately onboard with this, and thought it looked great? Or was there some skepticism, but someone said “trust me, people will love this, this is what a modern cabin looks like?”

I just don’t understand how you can commit to investing in a project that costs billions of dollars, reportedly get feedback from hundreds of customers, and still end up so far off the pulse of public sentiment.

Last week, Singapore Airlines unveiled its new cabins, which is an exciting development. Everything looked pretty great, except the new business class seat finishes, which seem terribly mismatched to the brand. The airline claimed it wanted something modern and progressive, but I’m not sure “suit with sneakers” is really the aesthetic that the public wanted (or that the chosen finishes actually reflect that).

Singapore Airlines leadership claims it’s now looking into possibly updating finishes, but I wouldn’t count on anything coming of that, given how far along this is.

What do you make of this Singapore Airlines business class design fiasco? And I’m still waiting for someone to please tell me that they love the design, and think it’s great!

#6192. Final Authority: The Pilot-Ceding Rule Every Air Traffic Controller Is Taught At Birth

On September 3, a JetBlue Airways captain climbing out of Fort Lauderdale faced an extraordinary choice: follow ATC instructions toward what appeared to be a severe thunderstorm, or take matters into his own hands. When the controller refused his requested alternative heading, citing conflicting traffic, the captain declared an emergency and began turning away.

The incident was notable enough that it was reported by View From The Wing at the time, which concluded that "declaring an emergency is no longer asking for permission: it is telling air traffic control what they are doing." It would also resonate just two months later when a Learjet 60 with nine people on board crashed after encountering severe turbulence in the same South Florida airspace.

It subsequently emerged that the ill-fated aircraft had a history of miscommunicating severe weather with ATC. The JetBlue confrontation demonstrated a fundamental principle of commercial aviation: although pilots ordinarily follow ATC clearances, ultimate operational responsibility belongs to the aircraft's captain.

Federal regulations recognize circumstances in which pilots may override instructions, sometimes without advance permission. From the Miracle on the Hudson to a deadly collision over Germany, aviation history reveals why that authority exists, and what can happen when pilots do not exercise it.

JetBlue flight B61971, operated by an Airbus A320 with the registration N715JB, departed Fort Lauderdale for Austin (AUS) 76 minutes late. During its climb, ATC assigned a 270-degree heading, but the crew believed that course would take them into severe weather. The pilots requested 250 or 240 degrees instead. The controller refused, explaining that other aircraft occupied the requested airspace and that her display showed a gap in the precipitation.

JetBlue's captain challenged that assessment, asking whether the controller intended to send them through a severe thunderstorm. The controller responded that she saw only "light precipitation" on the designated heading, to which the pilot responded:

"Not from the air, ma'am. So we declare an emergency, making a left turn heading two-six-zero for severe weather avoidance.”

ATC acknowledged the emergency, and the pilot subsequently reported new headings as the aircraft turned through 240 and 230 degrees. The pilot later explained to the controller that the severe weather on the previous heading was why they had declared an emergency, saying that "you do what you gotta do, we gotta do what we gotta do here."

The authority exercised by JetBlue's captain originates in 14 CFR 91.3. It establishes the pilot in command's ultimate responsibility and permits necessary deviations from Part 91 rules during emergencies requiring immediate action. Meanwhile, 14 CFR 91.123 provides explicit exceptions to ATC-clearance compliance, and 121.557 grants airline captains emergency operational authority.

These provisions do not permit arbitrary disregard of instructions. Controllers have substantial responsibilities of their own. They must maintain separation between aircraft, even when crews request weather deviations. FAA Order JO 7110.65 instructs controllers who cannot approve a requested deviation because of traffic to seek another solution that accommodates weather avoidance.

Necessary deviations from Part 91 permitted

Emergencies and TCAS advisories permit deviations

ATC seeks weather-safe alternatives while separating traffic

That helps explain the JetBlue controller's concerns: approving the crew's preferred heading without resolving conflicting traffic could have introduced another danger. These principles extend into airline procedures. Airline Flight Operations Manuals will document the captain's responsibility for safe operations and command over the crew​​​​​​.

Some manuals explicitly direct captains to declare emergencies in the event of severe weather that cannot otherwise be avoided. The FAA's foundational statement behind this is unequivocal, and concludes that "the pilot in command of an aircraft is directly responsible for, and is the final authority as to, the operation of that aircraft."

Getting the plane in the air is just the start...

Most disagreements never reach the emergency stage. Pilots typically request amended headings, routes, or altitudes, explaining why an assigned clearance is unsuitable. The word "unable" is used to communicate that an instruction cannot safely be accepted. The FAA explicitly encourages pilots to challenge instructions that would jeopardize safety.

Meanwhile, aviation training guidance emphasizes the importance of saying "unable" rather than reluctantly complying. That distinction emerged recently in an incident involving dangerous weather for United Airlines. Flight UA471's crew rejected a proposed route during pre-departure discussions in San Antonio (SAT), saying "we're unable [to take] the route" before ATC accepted an alternative.

Necessary action taken; ATC advised promptly

JetBlue's captain faced a more immediate airborne conflict, so he declared an emergency instead. History demonstrates why communicating an emergency clearly matters. On January 25, 1990, Avianca Flight 52 exhausted its fuel while approaching New York (JFK) after lengthy weather-related holding.

Despite communicating fuel concerns, the crew failed to convey the emergency adequately, and the Boeing 707 crashed, killing 73 people. The NTSB identified poor fuel management, inadequate emergency communication, and deficiencies in ATC traffic-flow management. The disaster illustrates the potentially fatal consequences of ambiguity.

One particularly dramatic confrontation occurred on May 4, 2010. American Airlines flight 2, a Boeing 767 arriving at JFK, was assigned Runway 22L despite winds from 320 degrees at 23 knots, gusting to 35. The captain considered the crosswind unacceptable and demanded Runway 31R. When ATC did not immediately accommodate the request, the crew declared an emergency, as follows:

Tower: “Alright I will pass it along, fly runway heading for now.”

AA 2 heavy: “Okay, we’re declaring emergency, we’re gonna land 3-1-right. We’re going to the left and then coming around.”

Tower: “American 2 heavy, just fly runway heading.”

Tower: “You say you’re declaring emergency?”

AA 2 heavy: “Three times I’ve told you that. Three times we’re declaring an emergency.”

Tower: “Okay, I just want to verify, I know you said if you didn’t get 3-1-right you have to declare an emergency. Okay, understand, fly runway heading and I gotta get you a turn!”

AA 2 heavy: “American 2 heavy, we are turning around to the left here and landing on 3-1. Remove everybody from our way. We’ve declared an emergency. We’re on a visual.”

Tower: “Alright, American 2 heavy, cleared to land, 3-1-right, 3-1-0 2-4 gusting to 3-4.”

AA 2 heavy: “Cleared to land, runway 3-1-right, American 2 heavy.”

A more recent incident demonstrates how differently such situations can unfold. In May last year, IndiGo flight 6E2142 requested an alternative routing near the India-Pakistan border, but military and civilian controllers denied the requested airspace access. The Airbus A321neo subsequently encountered hail and severe turbulence, damaging its nose before landing safely in Srinagar.

Strong crosswinds made the assigned JFK runway unacceptable to the crew.

Declared an emergency, rejected Runway 22L and landed on Runway 31R.

Incomplete weather information as the aircraft approached thunderstorms over Nebraska.

Encountered damaging hail, declared an emergency, and diverted to Denver.

ATC directed a weather deviation and issued a late descent restriction amid developing convection.

Encountered severe turbulence; six injured. Declared an emergency and landed at St. Petersburg.

Crew requested a deviation after encountering heavy rain and hail during climb from Milan.

Windshield cracked and aircraft damaged. Declared an emergency and diverted to Rome

ATC deferred a requested weather deviation until after a waypoint on approach to Atlanta.

Encountered severe turbulence, injuring 17. Declared a medical emergency.

ATC warned of nearby storms, but onboard displays showed no dangerous weather directly ahead.

Encountered hail and turbulence; aircraft substantially damaged but landed safely.

Requested weather deviations were denied by Indian military and Pakistani ATC authorities.

Encountered severe hail and turbulence, damaging the radome; landed safely in Srinagar.

Crew challenged proposed pre-departure routing through severe thunderstorms.

Rejected proposed routing, consulted dispatch and obtained an alternative clearance.

The underlying difficulty is that controllers and crews may have different, incomplete weather pictures. FAA guidance warns that ATC radar does not detect turbulence and that some precipitation displays can lag actual conditions by six minutes. Delta flight 1889's hail encounter also exposed failures in weather-information sharing. The FAA recommends avoiding severe thunderstorms by at least 20 miles (32 km), recognizing that dangerous turbulence can extend beyond visible precipitation.

Pilots consult dispatch and push for an alternate path as ATC initially points the flight directly into severe weather.

Perhaps the most famous demonstration of independent cockpit judgment occurred on January 15, 2009. After bird strikes disabled both engines of US Airways Flight 1549, Captain Chesley Sullenberger concluded that the Airbus A320 could not safely reach an airport. Despite ATC offering LaGuardia (LGA) and Teterboro Airport (TEB) landing options, he chose the Hudson River.

The extraordinary ditching saved all 155 people aboard, illustrating why the captain must ultimately judge an aircraft's capabilities. Two more recent incidents underscore that an ATC clearance doesn't guarantee a safe landing. In July 2017, Air Canada flight 759 nearly landed on an occupied San Francisco taxiway, initiating a go-around just before ATC also instructed one.

Rejected impractical airport options; ditched

Collision avoided; descended to roughly 60 feet

Collision avoided; separation approximately 150–170 feet

In February 2023, a FedEx Boeing 767 crew initiated a missed approach after spotting a Southwest Airlines 737 departing from the same Austin runway, avoiding a potentially catastrophic collision in dense fog. The examples differ from JetBlue's explicit refusal, but establish the same wider principle.

Pilots must assess risks from engine failures, runway obstructions, terrain, and conflicting traffic, even after receiving valid clearances. The FAA emphasizes that ATC authorization is not permission to conduct an unsafe operation. Sometimes the appropriate response is another request: sometimes it is an immediate go-around or emergency maneuver. The responsibility to recognize that distinction remains in the cockpit.

The consequences of conflicting instructions became devastatingly clear on July 1, 2002. Bashkirian Airlines Flight 2937 and DHL Flight 611 collided over Überlingen, Germany, killing all 71 people aboard the two aircraft. A controller had instructed the Bashkirian Tupolev Tu-154 to descend, while its Traffic Collision Avoidance System instructed the crew to climb.

Meanwhile, the DHL Boeing 757 received a coordinated TCAS instruction to descend. The DHL crew followed its automated advisory, but the Tupolev crew continued descending in accordance with ATC instructions, rather than the pilot-in-charge heeding the automated warnings. German investigators identified shortcomings in ATC operations and inconsistent procedures governing conflicting TCAS and controller instructions.

The disaster reinforced the importance of following TCAS resolution advisories, which take precedence over incompatible ATC vertical instructions. US regulations explicitly recognize TCAS advisories as an exception to normal clearance compliance. Nearly a quarter of a century later, the JetBlue captain faced a different danger, but one that also demonstrated why aviation cannot depend on unquestioning obedience.

Air traffic controllers coordinate movements and maintain separation, while captains retain responsibility for their aircraft's safe operation. The safest cockpit is therefore not one that follows every instruction, but the one that recognizes when an instruction can no longer be safely followed.

#6190. Amex Business Platinum Card Bonus: As High As 300K Points Welcome Offer

The Business Platinum Card® from American Express is one of the most perks-rich business cards out there, and is useful if you’re looking to earn Amex Membership Rewards points.

We’re currently seeing a massive elevated welcome offer on the Amex Business Platinum, making it an ideal time to apply. If you’re eligible for this card and the highest possible bonus, it’s absolutely worth taking advantage of, in my opinion.

Link: Learn more about The Business Platinum Card® from American Express

The Amex Business Platinum Card currently has a massive welcome offer that’s as high as 300,000 Membership Rewards points after spending $20,000 within the first three months. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Membership Rewards points to be worth 1.7 cents each. This means that to me, the 300,000 points are worth a staggering $5,100. As I see it, that’s basically the best welcome offer you’ll find on any card.

Let me emphasize that Amex uses a variety of factors when deciding what offer people are eligible for, including history of opening and closing cards with Amex, spending history with Amex, how many welcome offers people have earned, etc. So, how does this Amex Business Platinum Card bonus actually work?

You should find the highest possible Amex Business Platinum bonus through the above link. However, if you don’t, it can always be worth checking refer-a-friend links, opting in to targeted emails from Amex, or even using the CardMatch tool to see what you’re eligible for there.

That being said, don’t expect to get a higher offer through any of those sources, since offers are typically targeted based on the person, rather than the application method. However, it can always be worth checking back every so often, because the promotions people are targeted for can change over time.

The Amex Business Platinum bonus spending requirement is potentially significant, as it averages out to nearly $6,700 per month. However, there are lots of ways to be creative with reaching minimum spending, and to make a plan. You could time your application around some large upcoming business expenses (whether that’s an ad campaign or buying inventory), prepay for some items, and maybe even put some expenses on credit cards that you might otherwise pay for with cash. Of course make sure you pay off everything in full by the payment due date, so that you don’t get stuck paying high interest charges.

Upon completing minimum spending, bonus points will officially post after 8-12 weeks, though in practice, typically post much faster than that.

There are lots of great uses for Amex points, as they can be transferred to all kinds of useful airline and hotel partners. Also keep in mind that having this card lets you unlock the full value of Amex Pay With Points, potentially allowing you to get up to 1.54 cents of value per point toward the cost of airfare on a designated airline (this comes in the form of a 35% Pay with Points rebate, up to one million points per year). You could then use that redemption rate for all your linked Amex Membership Rewards cards.

Just to give a couple of examples of how much value those 300,000 Membership Rewards points could get you:

In line with Amex’s “once in a lifetime” rule, the welcome offer on the Amex Business Platinum Card isn’t available to those who currently have the card, or those who have had the card (or previous versions of the card) in the past. On top of that, Amex’s general card restrictions apply.

There are a few additional things to note:

Anecdotally, I find the Amex Business Platinum to be a pretty easy card to get approved for, and you can read about my experience applying here.

There’s not a consistent credit score you need to get approved for the Amex Business Platinum, though I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected, as it’s one of only many factors that impacts card approval.

The Amex Business Platinum Card has a $895 annual fee (Rates & Fees). While this isn’t the most rewarding card in terms of the return on spending, it does have a huge number of valuable perks, ranging from lounge access, to credits, to elite status.

The way I view it, the credits can help offset the Amex Business Platinum annual fee, and then the lounge access and other benefits are the icing on the cake. Here are just some of the benefits (Enrollment is required for select benefits):

Just to give a sense of the immense value, below is a basic rundown of the Amex Business Platinum credits, which should for many people help offset the annual fee (Enrollment is required for select benefits).

Of particular note is that the card offers up to $600 per year in hotel credits, in the form of a $300 credit semi-annually, and largely helps with offsetting the annual fee. The Hotel Collection requires a minimum two-night stay. Effective January 1, 2027, Fine Hotels + Resorts® bookings will require a minimum two-night stay to be eligible for the Hotel Credit.

This card offers all kinds of great perks that can help offset the annual fee, ranging from lounge access, to credits, to elite status, and more. You can even see what offer you’re eligible for on the card without a hard credit pull, so it’s worth seeing if you qualify, in my opinion.

#6189. American Airlines Pilot Arrested At Heathrow For Being Unfit To Fly And Having Cocaine

Every so often we’ll hear stories of pilots being arrested for showing up at the airport intoxicated. Well, here’s an even wilder story, about an American Airlines pilot who not only showed up at the airport unfit to fly, but also had cocaine on him.

View from the Wing flags a story about how on November 1, 2026, a 64-year-old pilot was arrested at London Heathrow Airport (LHR):

So this is sort of wild — not only was he under the influence of something (drugs or alcohol), but then he also had cocaine in his possession. That’s just next level irresponsibility.

It’s not clear how exactly all of this was discovered, in terms of the sequence of events. Was there just a random check, or was he acting erratically, authorities were alerted, and that’s when this all came to light? If so, it sounds like the first clue was how he was acting (which made him unfit to fly), and then presumably he was searched, which is when the cocaine may have been discovered.

This is just so beyond irresponsible. If he was already unfit to fly during boarding and had cocaine in his possession, was he going to consume that during the flight, or just take it home with him?

Keep in mind that in the United States, commercial pilots have to retire by their 65th birthday. So this guy was just weeks or months from retirement… what a sad way to end a career, as you can bet he won’t be flying again. One wonders if he was just trying to party a little before retirement, if this had been going on for some time, or what.

While the authorities haven’t identified the airline that this pilot works for (other than to say he works for a US airline), it’s not too hard to figure out. Based on his name (which I won’t post here, because he’s in enough trouble as is), it’s clear he’s an American Airlines pilot.

American had two flight cancelations out of Heathrow that day — one for flight AA85 to Chicago (ORD), and one for flight AA91 to Miami (MIA). It’s not clear which of those he was scheduled to fly on.

Under UK261 regulations, any passenger who ended up arriving at their final destination four or more hours late would be entitled to £520 ($690) in cash compensation. That’s on top of covering any reasonable expenses incurred. Admittedly some people may have been rebooked on other flights once this flight was axed, but at least a large percentage of passengers would presumably be eligible for this.

An American Airlines pilot who was close to retirement decided to end his career in a rather unfortunate way, as he was arrested at Heathrow for being unfit to fly, while also having cocaine in his possession. The lack of decent judgment shown here is beyond irresponsible, and I hope he gets the help he needs so he doesn’t ever endanger others in this way again. The good news for him is that he was within months of retirement anyway, so at least his “career” impact is pretty minimal.

What do you make of this American pilot being arrested?

#6186. Buy Etihad Guest Miles With 60% Bonus (2.0 Cents Each): Worth It?

Etihad Guest has just launched its latest promotion on buying miles, which is being marketed as the biggest offer of the year. With this, members can buy Etihad miles with a 60% bonus, which is an opportunity to acquire them for as little as two cents each.

Is that offer worth it? Let’s cover all the details, but I’ll say right away that I think this offer has fairly limited appeal, and you should only take advantage of this with a specific use in mind.

Link: Buy Etihad Guest miles with a bonus

Between 12:01AM GST on November 12 and 11:59PM GST on November 22, 2026, Etihad Guest is offering a bonus on purchased miles. The offer is tiered, and you get a bigger bonus the more miles you buy, as follows:

Note that purchased Etihad Guest miles post within 72 hours of completing the purchase (typically faster than that), and that purchased miles don’t count toward Etihad Guest elite status.

Etihad Guest ordinarily charges 3.2 cents per purchased mile, and there are no further taxes and fees. That’s before any bonuses or discount. With the 60% bonus, if you maxed out this promotion you’d receive a total of 320,000 Etihad Guest miles at a cost of $6,400, which is a rate of two cents per Etihad Guest mile.

Etihad Guest limits members to purchasing 200,000 miles per account per calendar year, before any bonuses. The exception is Etihad Guest Platinum members, who can purchase up to 300,000 miles per year, before any bonuses.

The current Etihad Guest buy miles promotion is described as the biggest offer of the year. To compare this to other offers we’ve seen so far this year, we’ve seen bonuses of 25-50% (2.56 cents to 2.13 cents per mile), as well as discounts of up to 35% (2.08 cents per mile).

As you can see, Etihad Guest’s current offer gives you the best cost per mile so far this year. However, Etihad isn’t exactly aggressive with selling miles, so it’s hard to get too excited about any of these amounts.

Etihad Guest mileage purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as an airfare purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach minimum spending, or otherwise a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending.

See this post for more on which credit cards are best for buying points.

There are lots of ways to redeem Etihad Guest miles. While the airline doesn’t belong to one of the major alliances, there are many ways to redeem the miles on both Etihad and on partner airlines.

Below you can find the award chart for travel exclusively on Etihad. The pricing is based on the one-way distance of travel. Note that these redemption rates are specifically for situations where there’s GuestSeat availability, which is Etihad’s capacity controlled, saver award space.

If you see higher award pricing than what’s listed below, that generally means there’s not saver award space, and redemptions won’t be a very good deal. Furthermore, in some situations you’ll find higher saver level award costs, including for travel in the carrier’s A380 first class.

Etihad Guest has a separate award chart for travel on partner airlines, which is also distance based, and you can find that below. This is based on the one-way distance, and you can’t mix airline partners on a single award.

The main reason to consider collecting Etihad Guest miles is because the program has access to a lot more Etihad award space than partner programs do. Partner programs, like American AAdvantage and Air France-KLM Flying Blue, typically only have access to a subset of premium cabin Etihad availability. Furthermore, if you want to fly in Etihad’s The Residence, your ticket needs to be issued by Etihad, so an Etihad Guest award redemption would qualify.

There are two major catches when it comes to Etihad Guest, in addition to not really having slam dunk redemption values:

I’d really only recommend buying Etihad Guest miles with a very specific use in mind, if you know what you’re doing.

Everyone will value mileage currencies differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Etihad Guest miles to be worth 1.1 cents each. I tend to value points pretty conservatively, and there are many ways to get more value from Etihad Guest miles than that.

Etihad Guest miles don’t expire as long as you have at least some account activity once every 18 months. Note that you can only reset the expiration of your miles by crediting a flight to the program every 18 months, so other activity wouldn’t help in that regard.

Keep in mind that there are many ways to earn Etihad Guest miles, so outright buying miles isn’t the only option. Etihad Guest also partners with select transferable points currencies. In the United States, you can move points to Etihad Guest at a 1:1 ratio from Bilt Rewards, Capital One, and Citi ThankYou, so that gives you quite a bit of flexibility.

Admittedly not everyone has access to credit cards in the United States, and some people may also prefer to just buy miles if they can acquire them at a reasonable cost.

Etihad Guest is selling miles with up to a 60% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy miles for as little as two cents each. This could be worth it if you have a specific use in mind, but Etihad Guest just seems rather unserious with its buy miles promotions, since the program isn’t that lucrative, in terms of redemption rates, and the policies for changing and canceling awards is also incredibly frustrating.

So for a vast majority of people, I’d recommend giving this offer a pass, unless you’ve done the math, and it checks out.

#6185. Allegiant Air Cancels 13 Routes To Major Vacation Destination: See Full List Now

Michael Take | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

Allegiant Air has flown to Myrtle Beach since 2009. Cirium Diio data shows that it was the ultra-low-cost carrier's third destination in South Carolina. It came after Columbia, the capital, and Greenville/Spartanburg, both first served 20 years ago. All flights to Columbia have now ended.

Myrtle Beach is renowned for being a family-friendly beach destination. It has tens of miles of white sand, along with being the so-called golf capital of the world. It is not a surprise that it had held much appeal for Allegiant for so long, at least until now, just as it is increasingly doing for Breeze.

Comparing the airline's schedule in 2026 with what is planned for 2027 shows that all of these routes are no longer scheduled. They were cross-referenced with what is listed on Allegiant's website, and all the routes were removed. The 13 markets are in nine states. While only two of the removed destinations are now served by another carrier, all nine states will still have flights, whether by Allegiant or a different operator.

US Department of Transportation data shows that Allegiant flew between Myrtle Beach and Atlantic City between March and August 2026. It had inherited the route from the now-defunct Spirit Airlines, which had served it for 29 years until early 2026. Allegiant transported 11,453 passengers and filled 80.5% of seats. While fare information is unavailable, the extremely short period shows that the route performed very poorly. Despite this, Breeze is keen, as flights started in October.

The cuts outlined above are only one part of Allegiant's story at Myrtle Beach. The ultra-low-cost carrier's booking engine currently extends to mid-May 2027. Between January and then, the airline plans to fly to nine places from Myrtle Beach: Akron/Canton, Albany, Allentown, Cincinnati, Columbus Rickenbacker, Harrisburg, Pittsburgh, Stewart, and Syracuse.

217 departures will be available on those nine routes through May 2027, down by 31% compared to January to May 2026. Seven of the markets will have fewer flights than they did, none more so than Akron/Canton, which Allegiant partly serves because Cleveland is only around an hour away. Departures in the first five months are down from 26 to just eight. In 2026, Allegiant served the market from March. Now it'll do so from May.

All of these routes begin in 2026 or 2027. Find them all here!

Most of the nine states will, of course, have flights to other places, rather than those dropped by Allegiant. Myrtle Beach will have flights to Illinois with American (Chicago O'Hare), Southwest (Chicago Midway), and United (O'Hare), while Indiana will be served by Southwest (Indianapolis).

Then there's Kentucky, with Allegiant flying to Cincinnati (the airport is in Kentucky, but the city is in Ohio), Maryland is linked with Southwest (Baltimore), Michigan's in the hands of Delta (Detroit), and New Jersey's served by Breeze (Atlantic City) and United (Newark).

New York has many routes from Allegiant (Albany, Stewart, Syracuse), American (LaGuardia), Breeze (Albany, Buffalo, Islip, Rochester, Stewart, Syracuse, Westchester), and Delta (LaGuardia). Ohio is served by Allegiant (Akron/Canton and Columbus Rickenbacker), Breeze (Akron/Canton and Columbus John Glenn), and Southwest (Columbus John Glenn). Finally, West Virginia will have flights by Breeze (Charleston) and Contour (Beckley and Parkersburg).

#6183. World Of Hyatt Brand Explorer: Free Night Awards For Staying At New Brands

There are several ways to earn World of Hyatt free night award awards. In this post, I’d like to talk about one of the often overlooked ways to earn Hyatt free nights, which is with World of Hyatt’s ongoing Brand Explorer promotion.

This offers World of Hyatt members the opportunity to earn free night awards for exploring Hyatt’s portfolio. Given the huge brand inflation that Hyatt has seen in recent years, this can potentially offer up to seven free night awards, and counting.

With World of Hyatt’s Brand Explorer promotion, you can earn a Category 1-4 free night certificate for every five unique Hyatt brands you stay at. When it comes to earning Hyatt Brand Explorer free night awards, here’s what you should know:

If you want to see how many Hyatt brands you’ve stayed at, you can do so either through the World of Hyatt website or mobile app. Just go to the “Brand Explorer” section, and there will be a display showing how many unique brands you’ve stayed at (including which ones), and also how many free night certificates you’ve earned.

When it comes to redeeming Hyatt Brand Explorer free night awards, here’s what you should know:

Of course you’ll maximize value with Brand Explorer by redeeming your free night award at an eligible Hyatt property when the cash rate would be as high as possible. World of Hyatt Category 4 properties can cost as much as 25,000 points per night, and in some situations, could retail for over $300 per night. So if you can find a hotel anywhere in that range, it’s a great way to maximize value.

Hyatt currently has 38 brands, which are as follows:

So as you can see, you’d need to stay at 35 brands to earn seven free night awards. If/when Hyatt adds two more brands, it’ll be possible to earn eight free night awards.

The World of Hyatt Brand Explorer offer is a fun way for the program to engage members and try to get them to try more brands. At least in one case it impacted where I chose to stay, because I do love checking this dashboard every so often, both to see the progress that I’m making, and be reminded of all the brands I’ve stayed at.

Even though I’ve had top tier status with World of Hyatt for over a decade and have now earned lifetime Globalist status, I haven’t even stayed at half of Hyatt’s current brand portfolio. As a matter of fact, I’ve only stayed at 13 of the 38 brands, so that’s just over one-third of properties.

Looking at the Hyatt brands I haven’t stayed at, most of them are all-inclusives, as that’s an area where Hyatt is growing significantly. However, in general this has limited appeal to me, based on the type of travel that I do. I’m sure I’ll knock out a few more brands in the coming years — maybe I’ll get to 15 brands, though I doubt I’ll make it to 20 brands in the foreseeable future.

With World of Hyatt’s ongoing Brand Explorer promotion, you can earn a free Category 1-4 free night awards for every five Hyatt brands you stay at. This is a way to earn up to seven free nights over time, based on Hyatt’s current portfolio of 38 brands. As Hyatt’s portfolio continues to grow, the opportunities to earn free nights continues to increase.

However, staying at Hyatt’s all-inclusive properties requires some effort, given that they’re not typically places you just drop into for a night.

Given how easy Hyatt makes it to track this, I’m curious — how many Hyatt brands have you stayed at? Which OMAAT reader has the record for the most brands?

#6182. The Nvidia Scandal Is a Warning Shot

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks to the media on the day he attends a meeting between Chinese Premier Li Qiang and U.S. business representatives at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, China, May 14, 2026.

Many Americans have their doubts about our cutting-edge AI, but as the drama now surrounding Nvidia seems to suggest, the Beijing regime does not feel the same way.

As a reminder, Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s CEO, put out a statement in which he admitted to having had an extramarital affair. The “other woman” has been identified in numerous reports as Alice Huang (no relation), a Chinese national.

Ms. Huang joined Megaspeed, a Singaporean company at around the time it moved into the data-center business shortly after a Biden-era tightening of export controls on advanced chips. She was briefly its managing director and sole shareholder and is believed to retain an executive role. She has not commented publicly on Mr. Huang’s admission. Her current whereabouts are unknown.

The principal focus of Megaspeed’s operations has been described as renting out computing power relying on Nvidia’s advanced chips (which it has bought in huge quantities) to its customers, enabling them to use it remotely. This is allowed, with exceptions, under U.S. law. What is not permitted is for the most advanced chips of this type to be exported to China. Little is known about Megaspeed’s client base (other than that it included Alibaba, the Chinese technology and e-commerce group), ultimate ownership (Ms. Huang had meanwhile sold her interest), or funding.

Megaspeed and, reportedly, Ms. Huang have attracted the attention of the U.S. authorities. Megaspeed has been accused of smuggling contraband chips to China. U.S. intelligence is said to have been aware of Ms. Huang’s relationship with Nvidia’s CEO and identified her as a Chinese spy, information reportedly passed on to senior officials in Washington. Megaspeed has denied the allegations against it (investigation of which was abruptly transferred from the Commerce Department to the Justice Department). Up until now, Nvidia has said that it found nothing amiss. China has rejected allegations of any spy plot.

Nvidia’s board has opened an investigation. Mr. Huang has said he will cooperate. The FBI is also digging, and Congress is taking a closer look. The investigations will reveal what they will reveal. Mr. Huang’s obligations as a husband are a matter solely for him and his family. As a CEO, however, it looks as if, to put it mildly, he has taken risks that he should not have. Unless he made some preemptive disclosures, the affair posed obvious intertwined questions about conflict of interest (Megaspeed was a large client after all), national security, and the threat of blackmail, all issues of which he must have been aware. Even if he has broken no laws, he appears to have put Nvidia into a position in which it should not have been. This story, as we know it so far, also raises issues about Nvidia’s corporate governance (who, if anyone, was keeping an eye on Huang?) and its relationship with the government. Who knew what and when, and what did they do, if anything, about it?

Handling this will be complicated by the nature of the AI “arms race” with China. It is a competition in which the U.S. is primarily participating through its private, not public, sector. To be sure, private companies were heavily involved in the Cold War’s arms and space races but mainly as government contractors, a relationship in which Washington, as the customer, set the agenda — and the rules. This time around, the private sector is leading the way, driven by its ambition to compete commercially. It is ahead of China to a degree that an effort dominated by the government would not match, but it’s a lead that Washington, if it mishandles its response to this mess, could all too easily undermine. China wants to win the AI race. So must we, and we must act accordingly.

That will require recognizing how critical Nvidia currently is. It supplies about 90 percent of the microchips used for training AI and 70 percent of those needed to run LLMs, and it is using its cash to play an important part in funding the development of America’s AI ecosystem. Its role will become less dominant — free markets and changing market leadership go hand in hand — but for the government to apply a wrecking ball to the company now would be madness.

There clearly need to be changes to the way that Nvidia, which is unusually dependent on one man, Jensen Huang, is run, and there needs to be accountability for what has taken place. But assuming his missteps turn out to be a matter of a terrible lapse and nothing more, the changes needed will probably be evolutionary rather than revolutionary. We should not want the disappearance of the executive energy that has made Nvidia the colossus it has become.

We do, however, need once again to examine what chips U.S. companies may sell to China. The efforts that the Chinese appear to be making to get hold of a U.S. product make the case for not selling it to them. Mr. Huang has argued that if the U.S. withholds more advanced chips, the Chinese will develop their own. They will try to do so anyway. Beijing’s instincts are autarkic. There is no sense in the U.S. making that task any easier.

Finally, it must be hoped that politicians do not exploit the fresh indignation now being stirred up about an already unpopular industry for their own purposes. To do so risks hobbling American AI. And that would hand Beijing a win far greater than anything that Megaspeed or Ms. Huang might have delivered.

My husband and I have always dreamed of visiting London, but we knew we wanted to do it the right way: comfortable flights and a chic hotel stay, with room left in our budget for things like afternoon tea, souvenirs and even a day trip.

All of that can sometimes require some pretty deep pockets, which is why we spent the past year allocating our spending strategically, using my to earn points toward both our flights and our hotel stay.

But like anyone on a budget, we wanted to get the most bang for our “point.” So when American Express last offered a 30% transfer bonus to the Virgin Atlantic Flying Club for eligible U.S. cardmembers, I knew I had to jump on the opportunity and book our trip asap. The good news? Amex is offering this same transfer bonus to Virgin again, now through Nov. 30, 2026.

Here’s how I made the most of the transfer bonus, including the redemptions I made and how you can do the same with the current offer.

First, let’s break down how the bonus works:

The American Express Membership Rewards® program is offering a 30% transfer bonus to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club for eligible U.S. cardmembers until Nov. 30, 2026. That means every 1,000 Membership Rewards points you transfer becomes 1,300 Virgin Points®. Terms apply. Note that Amex points must be transferred in multiples of 1,000, with a minimum of 1,000 points.

Now I’m no math whiz, but I do know that means 100,000 Membership Rewards points would convert to 130,000 Virgin Points, instead of the standard 1:1 ratio. That's one of the best transfer rates Amex offers.

Several Amex cards earn transferable Membership Rewards points, including:

Editor tip: If you’re new to transferring Membership Rewards, like I was, I highly recommend checking out our beginner-friendly guide that breaks down how to transfer Membership Rewards points to partners like Virgin step by step, along with any restrictions you need to be aware of.

The best part about Virgin as a transfer partner is its surprising breadth. You can redeem your points for flights on Virgin Atlantic, as well as stays at Virgin Hotels and cruise sailings with Virgin Voyages.

I had built up a solid balance of Membership Rewards points through a combination of the Gold Card's welcome offer and my everyday spending, but the limited-time window of that bonus meant I couldn't afford to think about it for too long.

I live in Central Florida, and luckily for me, Virgin Atlantic offers nonstop flights from Orlando

International Airport (MCO) to London's Heathrow Airport (LHR). However, Virgin Atlantic also flies nonstop to LHR from airports across the U.S., including:

Personally, I’ve always been curious about Virgin’s premium economy cabin after hearing so many great things about it from my fellow TPG colleagues. So for our outbound flight, we booked premium economy, which comes with perks like extra legroom and an elevated meal service.

It cost me 35,000 Virgin Points per person, plus taxes and fees. With the 30% bonus, I only needed to transfer 54,000 Amex points for the two of us, which means I saved 16,000 Amex points on the outbound leg alone.

Note that taxes, fees and charges apply in addition to the points price for reward flights in all classes. These vary depending on factors such as your destination and travel dates, and the applicable amount is shown at the time of booking.

From check-in to landing, the premium economy cabin proved to be the perfect balance of value and comfort. Extra touches like a dedicated check-in desk, a glass of bubbly after boarding, upgraded dining and amenity kits made the experience feel so special. The wide leather seats with extra legroom meant we arrived in London well-rested and ready to explore. I could see why so many people rave about it; it was the perfect middle ground between budget-friendly and comfortable.

The real splurge was our return flight, which turned out to hardly be a splurge at all because I found a nonstop Upper Class flight home from LHR to MCO for just 29,000 Virgin Points per person, plus taxes and fees. Thanks to the bonus, I only needed to transfer 46,000 Amex points total for two people. That's 12,000 Membership Reward points saved on an already incredible redemption. Needless to say, I felt like I’d won the lottery.

I’ll be the first to tell you that it doesn’t get any better than Virgin’s Upper Class for R&R on a nine-hour flight across the Atlantic. The direct-aisle-access seats converted into lie-flat beds, and the amenity kits were well curated. Not to mention that the dining and inflight service made me feel like, well, royalty.

By the time we touched down in Orlando, I had slept through most of the flight, which is a rarity for me as a nervous flyer. We arrived home feeling restored rather than depleted.

Combined, our flights cost us 128,000 Virgin Points plus taxes and fees, which took 100,000 Amex points to cover. The transfer bonus saved my husband and me 28,000 Membership Rewards points across both flights, and we used them to redeem on Virgin Red for a rewards stay at Virgin Hotels London-Shoreditch.

Once I had committed to the Virgin Atlantic booking, staying at Virgin Hotels London-Shoreditch was a no-brainer with that 30% transfer bonus. And yes, when you transfer Membership Rewards points to the Virgin Atlantic Flying Club, you can use them toward a stay at a Virgin Hotels property.

Editor tip: Once you’ve transferred your Membership Reward points to Virgin,  check out our easy-to-follow guide to booking Virgin Hotels with Virgin Points.

On our dates, the stay came out to about 60,000 Virgin Points per night. For our four-night stay, I was looking at 240,000 points in total, which felt like a lot to give up. With the 30% transfer bonus, though, I only needed to transfer 185,000 Membership Rewards points, which was much easier to wrap my head around.

When I booked the hotel, I had a feeling using my points would be well worth it, and from the moment we arrived at Virgin Hotels London-Shoreditch, my suspicions were confirmed. The hotel sits in trendy East London, far enough from the crowds and tourist traps, but close to the Old Street Tube station for easy access to activities and dining across the city. It’s also a convenient 10-minute walk from Liverpool Street Station, which has direct access to LHR.

The hotel has quintessential Virgin design, with red accents everywhere, from the lobby carpets to the Smeg fridges in the guest rooms. Beyond the rooms, the property has a rooftop pool for the warmer months and a retro hi-fi listening bar called Hidden Grooves, which serves creative cocktails that are perfect after a long day exploring London.

As for how it compares to cash pricing, a comparable room size runs around $450-$550 per night. Our four-night stay on Virgin Points was equivalent to saving roughly $2,000 in cash, which suddenly made the Amex transfer bonus feel like money in the bank.

With our flights and hotels covered by points, we had cash to spend on our most anticipated experiences in London. Here are a few of my favorite trip highlights:

My Membership Rewards transfer to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club covered nearly every big-ticket item on our London trip: flights in both directions, including a lie-flat Upper Class seat home, and four nights at Virgin Hotels London-Shoreditch. With the 30% transfer bonus stretching every point further, we were able to spend our cash on experiences, dining and souvenirs.

If you've been sitting on a stash of Membership Rewards points, this is one of the best ways to use them right now, and you don’t need to go to London. Virgin Atlantic also flies nonstop from the U.S. to Manchester and Edinburgh and connecting through Heathrow opens up destinations like Barbados, Cape Town, Dubai, Mumbai and the Maldives.

Your points aren't limited to flights, either. You can put them toward a stay at Virgin Hotels or even a Virgin Voyages cruise. Just keep in mind that the 30% transfer bonus, available to eligible U.S. cardmembers, ends Nov. 30, 2026, so whether you're dreaming of a lie-flat seat across the Atlantic or days in the sun at sea, now is the time to book your next trip.
