#6178. Air Algerie Business Class Review: An Odd Avion Express Airbus A320 Wet Lease

For the next portion of my Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, I flew Air Algerie’s Airbus A320 business class on the one-hour flight from Algiers (ALG) to Tunis (TUN). Okay, Air Algerie doesn’t actually operate A320s, so this flight was operated by Lithuanian and Maltese charter operator Avion Express (which Air Algerie is really bad at disclosing during the booking process).

I mean, what can one really say about this flight, especially after coming off of Air Algerie’s A330neo business class, which was possibly the worst long haul business class I’ve ever flown? Truth be told, for a short haul flight this wasn’t terrible, but it also wasn’t good. It was just… whatever. As an aviation geek, I always do love a wet lease adventure!

As I explained in the last installment, I booked an attractive one-way business class cash fare on Air Algerie, even though it didn’t start or end where I actually wanted to go. 😉 I booked the following in business class for $1,171 in cash:

10/03 AH2701 Montreal to Algiers departing 4:10PM arriving 5:00AM (+1 day)10/04 AH4000 Algiers to Tunis departing 7:10AM arriving 8:30AM

So in the last installment I reviewed Air Algerie’s A330neo business class, and then this installment is my review of the connecting flight.

I’ve already reviewed the Air Algerie VIP Lounge Algiers, which gives strong furniture store vibes and is nothing remarkable, but is still much better than Air Algerie’s onboard experience.

My flight to Tunis was scheduled to depart at 7:10AM, and my boarding pass indicated that boarding would start at 5:40AM. Yes, 90 minutes before departure… for an Airbus A320. Not surprisingly, that was completely inaccurate. I get that airlines don’t want people to miss flights, but I do find it frustrating when airlines don’t actually tell you when you should realistically be at the gate.

Anyway, my flight was departing from gate nine, roughly a five-minute walk from the lounge. Algiers Airport is fairly pleasant — it feels sterile and there’s not much to it, but compared to some other airports in the region, it isn’t half bad. But of course let me remind everyone that nothing holds a candle to Cairo Airport (CAI), easily one of the world’s finest facilities. 😉

I showed up at the departure gate plenty early, but even by 6:10AM (30 minutes after the alleged boarding start time), there wasn’t actually anyone at the gate.

The crew showed up at around 6:20AM, and boarding actually started at 6:35AM. The boarding process was rather strange on a variety of levels.

For one, before boarding started, the gate agent and security staff walked onto the jet bridge and then lit a cigarette and smoked. Nice… real professional.

Second, when boarding did start, it was just a free for all, with no priority give to business class passengers.

Third, there were three separate passport and boarding pass checks on the jet bridge by airport police. So first the gate agent checked documents, then upon entering the jet bridge a security officer checked both, then 100 feet later another security officer did the same, and then at the door of the plane, another security officer checked. After all that hard work protecting us, they definitely deserve a cigarette!

At the forward door to the plane I was greeted by the crew, and then headed toward my seat. I was flying on an 18-year-old Avion Express Airbus A320 with the registration code 9H-AMJ. While Avion Express is a Lithuanian company, this plane was registered in Malta.

This A320 has seen quite some things, as it started its career in 2008 at Wizz Air Ukraine, then in 2015 it moved to the main Wizz Air fleet when the Ukrainian subsidiary shut down, and then in 2021 it was taken over by Avion Express. Since then, it has flown on a wet lease basis with carriers like Eurowings, British Airways, Viva, and more.

For those not familiar with the concept of wet leasing, this is when an airline leases out its plane to another airline, including the crews. So while it’s sold just like any other Air Algerie flight, and the catering is like any Air Algerie flight, the crew and planes are from Avion Express.

This Avion Express A320 had a total of 180 seats, spread across 30 rows in a 3-3 configuration. Unfortunately unlike most of Air Algerie’s own planes, this one didn’t have a dedicated business class cabin with different seats. Instead, the first three rows were designated as business class, and they just had economy seats with blocked middles. That means business class had the capacity for 12 passengers.

I assigned myself seat 3F, the window seat on the right side in the third (last) row. This was a pretty old school cabin, which is a double edged sword. On the plus side, this meant seats were well padded, which you don’t typically find nowadays, given the emphasis on slimline seats.

Legroom was okay when you consider these are really economy seats, so it could’ve been worse.

The seat had a standard tray table, which folded down from the seat in front.

Given how old school the cabin was, it definitely wasn’t in very good condition, though. I mean, just look at the liner inside the window, and how that was coming apart.

Also, given the age of the cabin, it was clear that nothing had really been updated — there were no power ports, there was no Wi-Fi, and there was no streaming entertainment. That’s of course not a huge issue for such a short flight, but I’m just trying to help people manage expectations here.

The overhead console was typical for an A320, and had individual air nozzles and reading lights.

The cabin stayed really empty — there were only two other commercial passengers, and then one pilot who seemed to be commuting to Tunisia, for whatever reason.

Boarding was really efficient, and wrapped up by 6:55AM, as the flight wasn’t very full. That was still 15 minutes before the scheduled departure time. Before departure, the crew came around with juice or water as pre-departure drinks. I opted for a water, and was also given a packaged refreshing towel.

Ironically enough, on this flight the safety demonstration was exclusively performed in English (compared to my previous Air Algerie flight, where it was in French and Arabic, but not in English).

At 7AM the main cabin door closed, and at 7:05AM we began our pushback (sorry for the quality of the pictures, as the windows were super dirty)…

On the taxi out, we saw another Avion Express A320, which looked identical to ours (we also had an all-white A320).

There were quite a few Air Algerie planes parked on the ramp, as very few seemed to actually be at gates. I’m not sure if Air Algerie’s aircraft utilization is just terrible, or what.

By 7:25AM we made it out to runway 23, and were immediately cleared for takeoff.

Our climb out was smooth, and I loved the views on departure… I wish I could’ve actually visited Algiers, but the visa situation is complicated (and after my review, I’m not sure they’d be happy to have me anyway). 😉

The seatbelt sign was turned off around five minutes after takeoff. At that point the crew closed the curtain between the cabin and galley, and got started with the service.

On this morning flight, breakfast was served. There was no choice, but I was served a hot dish with scrambled eggs, veggies, and some sort of meat. There was also a yogurt, a croissant, and a pastry, and additional bread rolls were offered (though I passed).

It sure seems like Air Algerie instructs Avion Express flight attendants to not deviate from their service protocol, which is to say that everything must simply be thrown on the tray, with zero effort put into presentation. 😉

So I couldn’t help but reorganize the tray a little bit, to make it look a little more presentable.

Drinks were also offered. I asked for a coffee, and it was a rather disgusting powdered coffee that I didn’t at all enjoy.

Before the descent, I checked out the lavatory, located at the front of the cabin. It was very basic and worn, though at least it wasn’t dirty.

Since this was a wet lease, the flight attendants onboard worked for Avion Express. I couldn’t actually figure out what country they were from (and they weren’t really friendly enough that I felt like being conversational). But anyway, they went through the motions, and weren’t rude, and they spoke a little bit of English (more than the Air Algerie crew on my previous flight).

There was also one Air Algerie flight attendant onboard, I guess to “oversee” the service, as is common with wet leases like this. In this case, he just plopped down in a business class seat and relaxed for most of the flight.

Around 30 minutes after takeoff, at roughly the halfway of the flight, the captain made an announcement, informing us we were at an altitude of 10,700 meters (35,000 feet), and that we’d be descending in around five minutes. Sure enough, we started our descent as planned, and the seatbelt sign was turned on 10 minutes after that.

The views on approach were gorgeous. Tunis is of course a coastal city on the Mediterranean Sea, so the views are tough to beat. I fondly remember my visit to Tunisia around a decade ago.

On our approach, we ended up flying out over the Mediterranean, and then circling back to land toward the south.

We ended up touching down on runway 19 at 8:25AM.

From there we had a short five-minute taxi to our arrival gate, where we pulled in at 8:30AM next to an Etihad A321LR (probably the nicest plane that serves the airport).

From there I cleared transit security, and had an extended layover, before connecting to Marseille (MRS) in Tunisair economy (due to a downgrade from business class).

My Air Algerie flight operated by an Avion Express A320 was perfectly whatever. For an hour-long flight, I thought the meal was quite good. However, the Avion Express A320 wasn’t terribly inspiring in terms of its modernness, seating, amenities, or service. So yeah, I don’t really have strong feelings on this one, other than appreciating that the flight was at least on schedule.

What do you make of Air Algerie business class, operated by an Avion Express A320?

I had a similar experience flying them from Algiers to Constantine. Biz class is just a coach seat (window or aisle) with the middle seat blocked off. Fairly mediocre experience but still miles ahead of Royal Air HardasaRoc, I mean, Maroc. Now that was a craptacular experience.

The tray arrangement does seem to confirm my suspicion they are round-trip catering their TATL flights…!

Well, this crew was better in hygiene than the last crew. At least, they know to put the bread on a plate rather than on the tray. Also, the food seemed much better.

#6177. The Logic-less Crusade That Just Killed a Data Center

Do activists believe that the $5 billion that would have been spent on this project is just waiting to be allocated elsewhere?

An aerial view of a 49.5-megawatt, three-level data center under construction in Vernon, Calif., April 14, 2026. Inset: Taylor Frazier McCollum

Mario Tama/Getty Images, Screenshot via Electric Llama/YouTube

Meet Taylor Frazier McCollum. McCollum just led a successful movement to block the construction of a $5 billion data center campus in Prince George’s County, Md. Simultaneously, McCollum is upset that her county’s government will not pay for a new roof for her grandfather’s home. Somehow, McCollum cannot see the connection between these two things. In an interview with NPR, she explained that the data center project prompted her political “awakening” and boasted that “so many people are depending on this fight to be successful.”

Are they? Prince George’s County is not in good shape. It has a budget deficit of more than $130 million. Unemployment is high. Last year, the Six Flags amusement park there closed permanently, and in the next few years, the Washington Commanders NFL team intends to move out. The FBI is also trying to leave. McCollum’s father believes that his daughter is a hero in the mold of Medgar Evers, who was killed trying to integrate Mississippi’s schools, or of Martin Luther King. “People like Taylor,” he says, “jump out here so the people behind them get to make progress.”

#6175. Global Airlines Liquidating: The Senseless A380 Dream Finally Dies

Over the past few years, I’ve extensively covered Global Airlines, the strange “airline startup” that had a single Airbus A380, with which it wanted to bring back the “golden age” of travel. The carrier’s A380 has been parked since the spring of 2025, and just several months ago, I covered how the company faced several winding up petitions. Well, there’s now an update, which seems long overdue…

Public records in the UK show that Global Airlines has finally been given winding up orders, which is the equivalent of liquidation. This is in response to a petition that was filed on May 29, 2026, and a court approved that order on November 4, 2026. This has only been added to public records today, as there seems to be a one week period between when these decisions are made, and when they’re published for the public.

This means that a government officer from the Insolvency Service will now become the liquidator, and take control of the company, investigate its affairs and the conduct of directors, and collect whatever assets still exist for creditors. This means that the directors no longer have control of the company.

What’s amazing about this entire story is that in the spring of 2025, the company actually operated two roundtrip flights to New York out of Europe, for reasons that most of us couldn’t really make sense of. For that matter, this was part of a wet lease agreement with Portuguese charter company Hi-Fly, given that Global Airlines lacked its own operating certificate.

James Asquith, founder of Global Airlines, gate crashes travel guru Simon Calder's interview with Mike Graham.@james_asquith: "Did you get a cupcake?"@Iromg | @SimonCalder pic.twitter.com/etMVj1TcPu

Shortly after the A380 operated those flights, it entered long term storage, as it needed to undergo heavy maintenance, which costs millions of dollars. The company’s founder, James Asquith, had insisted that the reason the plane was parked for so long was due to delays with being able to get heavy maintenance.

Just months ago, Asquith suggested that the airline would be flying to the Maldives before the end of 2026, despite no progress having been made on the heavy maintenance front.

A post shared by Robyn Asquith (@robynasquith)

Obviously on the surface, the whole Global Airlines thing sounds a bit odd. But let me simply say that the public knows only a tiny fraction of what was really going on here. That’s true both in terms of what Asquith was showing investors to get them onboard with the concept, and also what he claimed the goals for the company were.

My skepticism with this concept wasn’t because I don’t like to see other people succeed, or because I’m against innovation, or anything like that. Instead, it’s because things aren’t always what they seem, and when you’re raising millions of dollars of other people’s money and selling them a dream, there has to be some chance of that actually becoming a reality.

Keep in mind that in 2025, Asquith appeared on The Times’ 40 richest people under 40 list, which claimed he had a net worth of £183 million, making him richer than Adele. Right.

I’d encourage those who just went along with Asquith to be a little introspective here. For example, when you have publications like SimpleFlying that publish things about Global Airlines without even an ounce of skepticism, and then you have people like Captain Chris who latch on to people like Asquith as if they’re Richard Branson (which he literally compared him to, while pointing out that he was proving the doubters wrong), that’s a problem.

A post shared by Captain Chris | Aviation Life (@captainchris)

Many people lost many millions of dollars on this venture. Now, I’d also encourage them to perhaps be a bit more careful next time. And if you just want to make a donation to someone with no expectation of any return, I’m also happy to wire you my bank account details. 😉

It’s the end of the road (or runway) for Global Airlines, as the A380 “airline” has had its winding up petition approved, meaning the company will now be liquidated. It was only a matter of time before this was going to happen, so I don’t think anyone will be surprised. Hopefully one day the entire story can come to light…

What do you make of Global Airlines liquidating?

Alaska Airlines' largest hub, Seattle (SEA), is about to gain four new nonstop domestic flights, as the airline adds services to Charlotte, Des Moines, Jacksonville and Norfolk. These routes will all operate daily.

According to aviation blogger Enilria, the oneworld carrier will expand its domestic reach from Washington State, following the airline's announcement of plans to operate flights to Guadalajara in Mexico and nonstop services from Anchorage to Tokyo.

Beginning on June 10, 2027, Alaska will take on American Airlines, with both carriers connecting the East to the West. This will be Alaska's only service to Charlotte, where it will go head-to-head with American, which holds more than 89% market share at the airport.

Flights from Seattle will depart for Charlotte in the morning for a late-afternoon arrival, while return flights leave in the early evening for a late-night arrival back in Seattle. The route will be served year-round.

Alaska will fly its Boeing 737-900ER on the service to Charlotte, whereas American typically operates the Airbus A321 on its service to Seattle. Below is Alaska's schedule to Charlotte:

Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA)

Charlotte Douglas International Airport (CLT)

Charlotte Douglas International Airport (CLT)

Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA)

On the same day that Alaska debuts its new service to Charlotte, the airline will also begin its year-round service to Norfolk International Airport (ORF). Alaska will become the only airline serving the route, with the service expected to operate daily. Flights will depart from Seattle at 7:30 AM each morning, with return flights departing at 5:01 PM. Flights will be operated by the airline's Boeing 737 aircraft.

Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA)

Seattle-Tacoma International Airport(SEA)

Jacksonville will also be on the airline's menu, as the airline plans to introduce nonstop flights from June 24. The route will become the airline's longest domestic service, covering 2,439 miles (3,924 kilometers). Service will take five and a half hours from Seattle.

Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA)

Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA)

These will be brand new routes from Seattle, with no other airline having operated them previously.

Late night Seattle departures connect to early morning arrivals in Guadalajara three times weekly aboard 737-800.

The last route Alaska announced is its nonstop flight to Des Moines. These nonstop services to Iowa will begin on June 24, and are set to operate year-round. This will be the first time an airline has served the city pair. Flights will operate on the airline's Embraer E175 regional jets, which can seat up to 70 passengers.

Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA)

Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA)

No other airline operates this route; however, other West Coast gateways include Burbank, Orange County, Portland, and Los Angeles (LAX).

#6173. Wild: Stolen Delta Bag Tracked From JFK To DC Bus Stop, Thief Nabbed By Police

It’s not totally uncommon to see bags stolen (or perhaps in some cases accidentally taken) from baggage claim belts at airports. In the past that was basically a lost cause, but thanks to things like AirTags, they can often be tracked.

Here’s an absolutely wild version of such a story, where someone in the miles & points community had their bag stolen, and then someone else tracked it down… hundreds of miles away, and with the help of police!

JT Genter is Editor-in-Chief of AwardWallet and a member of the miles & points community who travels full time. On Tuesday, November 10, 2026, he took to social media to share that his checked bag had been stolen off the Delta baggage claim belt at New York Kennedy Airport (JFK) Terminal 4.

He filed a Delta missing bag claim and police report, and pointed out how “so many irreplaceable memories” were lost in the bag, including all his clothing, medicines, all his toiletries, etc. And he claimed that Delta agents didn’t seem like they gave a you-know-what.

God. So many irreplaceable memories lost in that bag. All of my clothing. Medicines. All my toiletries. Literally so many of my worldly possessions stolen right off Delta's baggage claim belt.And @Delta agents couldn't give less of a shit. Acted like it must happen all the time

That’s obviously incredibly frustrating, though this is a story that had a happy ending less than 24 hours later. JT did have a tracker in his bag, so could keep an eye on the movements of the bag, but he just didn’t say so initially. Apparently the person had pretty quickly taken Amtrak down to DC.

But this is where the story gets truly wild. Jamie Larounis, an Upgraded Points contributor and another member of the miles & points community, coordinated with JT to help. Let me just share Jamie’s version of events:

This might be a story for the history books. Man steals backpack in NY. He takes Amtrak train to DC. I decided to play detective and found the thief with the backpack sitting at a bus station. He boards a bus, but luckily I caught the bus number. I found 2 extremely helpful cops to assist and they found the thief a few blocks away and they nabbed him. They asked me to get in the cop car to ID the thief, and we headed to the police station to retrieve the items.

Gotta say, I didn’t have being in a Metropolitan Police cop car on my bingo card today, but with a little perseverance we got this thief locked up!!! Huzzah!

And by "we", I mean @TheForwardCabin! Jamie used the Tile tracking location to get a visual on our bag and found DC police who were ready to protect and serve.What an incredible end to this story!https://t.co/LvFthwBMqt

When asked what was missing from the bag after it was recovered, JT shared that the guy ditched some clothing, supplies, and custom medical equipment, plus “irreplaceable memories.”

When you consider the volume of bags that are checked, obviously a fair number get lost, stolen, etc. In theory, stealing a bag from a baggage claim belt is really easy — you just take it and leave. However:

Publicly, we of course don’t know anything about this thief. Are we to assume that he wasn’t actually flying, and was just there to steal a bag? And of all the bags he could steal, why did that black backpack catch his eye? And was he planning to travel to DC anyway, and if so, was that the plan all along, or was that just the “escape” plan with the stolen goods?

I recognize that people stealing bags off of baggage claim belts probably aren’t the most sophisticated criminals, but in this day and age, you’d think that checking every pocket of the bag for a tracker would be a best practice, given how common they are.

A traveler had their backpack stolen off of a baggage claim belt at JFK after a Delta flight. Fortunately he had a tracker, which showed that the bag was taken down to DC on Amtrak. After posting about this online, someone else coordinated and played detective, and found someone with the bag at a bus station in DC, and with the help of police, it was recovered.

It’s nice when a story like this has a positive ending, and it’s also a good reminder to put some sort of a tracking device in your bag, for situations where your bag gets lost or stolen.

What do you make of this checked bag recovery mission?

#6172. Why Policy Will Make a Comeback in 2028

Within both major parties, dramatic ideological battles will play out in the presidential race.

With the midterms now behind us, the political world has already shifted to speculation about the next presidential race. While I am not quite ready to make any horse race bets, I will venture to make an even bolder prediction: 2028 will be the election when policy makes a comeback.

At risk of being accused of romanticizing the past, I will freely acknowledge that there was never any golden age in which presidential campaigns were focused on sober-minded discussions about the finer points of policy. Go back through the decades, and in every election, you will find complaints about how elections were much more focused on personalities and trivial matters than serious issues.

American Airlines is planning to add more flights from Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), as part of a “gradual build” at its West Coast hub.

The Fort Worth-based carrier said it's about to add more LAX service to its schedule, with a focus on places executives describe as “important markets.”

It’s not clear whether that means entirely new routes or more frequent service on existing ones.

But either way, it comes after a long stretch where American seemed to focus far more of its attention on other parts of the country.

After the pandemic, the airline doubled down on its Sun Belt hubs, fortifying its strongholds in Dallas, Charlotte and Miami.

More recently, American reignited a longstanding Chicago turf war with United Airlines when it rapidly reinstated flying at O’Hare International Airport (ORD).

It looks like LAX will be its next project.

“We’re going to grow," American chief commercial officer Nat Pieper said, speaking this week at an industry conference. "We’re going to tailor a schedule to the local market."

American has a smaller presence today in Southern California than it did several years ago.

This year, the carrier will operate about 32% fewer flights than it did in 2019, according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium.

That’s a significant drop-off at LAX, which is one of the nation’s most competitive airports — and the only where each of the “big three” legacy carriers operates a hub.

By contrast, top L.A. rival Delta Air Lines has solidified its place as the airport’s top carrier, and plans operate its largest-ever schedule there next year.

United Airlines has also signaled it has future growth aspirations at LAX.

Speaking earlier this year, United’s top network planner, Patrick Quayle, lamented the fact that the airport is United’s only hub where there’s another airline with a larger presence.

“I don’t like being No. 2,” Quayle said during a company event at LAX in March. “And so I will, today, put Delta on notice here in L.A. — we will be No. 1, as well.”'

Pieper said the carrier needs to start by catering more to local Los Angeles customers — not just using the airport as a hub to route connecting traffic.

Doing that, he acknowledged, will likely require AA to offer a longer list of unique destinations.

Today, for instance, the carrier only serves four long-haul cities from LAX: London, Tokyo, Sydney and Auckland.

“People don’t only want to fly domestically. They want to go to Latin America. They want to go to Europe. They want to go to Asia,” Pieper said on stage this week at the Skift Aviation Forum in New York. “We need to be able to serve that with our own airplanes.”

United is clearly following that formula. The carrier already serves more than a half-dozen transpacific destinations from Southern California — and will expand next year with a new route to Osaka.

Delta, for its part, is also pointing to LAX as a linchpin of its Pacific growth aspirations, having launched nonstops to Hong Kong and Melbourne within the past year. New flights to Manila will begin in 2027.

Delta’s Los Angeles growth is also thanks, in part, to massive infrastructure investments the carrier has made at the hub which, among other things, is the only airport that's home to two Delta One Lounges.

American’s LAX digs, meanwhile, are still a construction zone.

The carrier had to consolidate its presence at the airport last year to make way for a rebuild of the airport's Terminal 5.

American will grow at a "gradual" pace, Pieper said, until its LAX facilities are "ready to roll." That's expected to happen in late 2028, at which point the carrier will have access to 30 gates.

“Our facility will be as good as anybody’s,” he said.

That, along with more flights — plus connectivity to American's Pacific partners like Qantas and Japan Airlines— have the airline more bullish about its hub that's grabbed far fewer headlines in recent years.

“You combine all those things together,” Pieper added, “I think we’re going to have a compelling offering there.”

#6169. Beond Airlines Suspends Flights Again: Will They Resume In December?

Back in April 2026, we saw Beond Airlines suspend all scheduled operations for the summer, as the airline claimed it would resume flights as of October. Then in October, it announced it would return in December. Is that actually happening now, or what exactly is going on?

Beond Airlines launched operations in 2023, and it brands itself as the world’s first premium leisure airline. The company is headquartered in Dubai, but primarily operates flights to and from the Maldives. I reviewed the airline in 2024, and the onboard product was super pleasant. The airline currently has a fleet of two aircraft, including one A319 and one A321.

Anyway, in mid-April 2026, the company announced that it would suspend its scheduled operations for the entire summer. The airline promised to resume flights in October, for the winter season.

Then in October, the airline announced that it would suspend operations through November 30, 2026, meaning it will resume flights as of December 1, 2026. Interestingly, the airline has promised to provide a schedule update by November 12, 2026, but that date has now come and gone, and there was no update.

So I guess it remains to be seen if we actually see a resumption of flights as of December, or if the timeline will get pushed back again. The company does have a section on its travel updates page with FAQs, and one of the questions is “will the dates change again?” The answer is “we chose dates we are confident in,” but also notes that “if anything changes, you will hear from us first.”

Beond Airlines does have its “commitment” to customers when plans change, which includes the ability to change destinations or travel dates, receive a travel credit valid for 18 months, or to receive a full refund. A change of destinations or dates, plus a travel credit, isn’t worth a whole lot for an airline that keeps pushing back its relaunch.

Interestingly, but perhaps not surprisingly, earlier this year the airline deleted its customer promise webpage, which used to guarantee rebooking on another airline in business class in the event a flight is canceled, or else the airline would offer a free flight. That page is now gone, and there’s no mention of rebooking on another airline.

So the airline will “support you every step of the way,” unless you actually want to take the vacation you booked, in which case you’re out of luck (which is less than ideal, given that many Maldives properties have very strict cancelation policies).

While Beond Airlines’ business plan was questionable under the best of circumstances, the crisis of this year makes matters worse:

So I feel bad for Beond, and I’m not trying to do a “told you so, I was right” thing, because these are of course exceptional circumstances. The thing that made me suspicious about Beond for so long is that the airline would repeatedly make outlandish growth announcements, only to rarely follow through on them. That’s neither here nor there, though.

Keep in mind that since operations were initially suspended in April, we’ve seen some interesting developments:

My assumption is that Saudi Arabia is to some extent funding the Red Sea flights, given how the country is throwing money at any airline willing to fly there. However, one wonders if that’s enough money to make the math work, or if Beond even has the general funding right now to keep things operating.

It’s just all so strange, because it feels like half of the announcements from Beond Airlines are really targeting prospective investors, constantly promoting how it’s going to open new subsidiaries all over the world, launch dozens of new routes, etc.

As I said in April, I didn’t think it was a sure bet that flights would resume in October. Now we’ll see if flights actually resume in December.

In the spring of 2026, all-business class airline Beond suspended scheduled operations through October 2026. That timeline has come and gone, and now the airline claims it’ll resume operations as of December 2026. Over the summer, we learned that the airline wasn’t paying many staff for months, and the airline is now pivoting to operating service via Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea Airport.

We’ll see what happens in the coming weeks. Presumably the Red Sea service gets the airline some money from the Saudi government, but it remains to be seen if that’s enough to keep this operation afloat.

It’s understandable that the current situation is really challenging, between the price of jet fuel, plus overall sentiment about the Middle East. However, I have to imagine the airline didn’t have great financial health before this whole mess started, and suspending flights in some ways only makes things even worse.

How do you see this playing out for Beond?

#6168. How Many Crew Members Does It Take To Fly A KC-135 Stratotanker?

First flown in 1956, the Boeing KC-135 Stratotanker has spent decades refueling US military aircraft in flight. Despite its age, it remains a major part of the United States Air Force's tanker fleet, supporting fighters, bombers, and other aircraft on missions around the world. But how many people does it actually take to operate an aircraft responsible for such an important job? The answer raises some interesting questions about how the Stratotanker was designed and how its crew responsibilities have changed over the years.

The KC-135's crew arrangement is not quite as straightforward as it might seem. Its refueling missions require close coordination between the cockpit crew and the operator responsible for transferring fuel, while other missions can bring additional personnel aboard. Its history also raises questions about why it differs from commercial aircraft of the same era and how its crew compares with that of the newer KC-46 Pegasus. Looking at these differences helps explain how the Stratotanker has continued to serve for so many decades.

For a normal refueling mission, according to the US Air Force's KC-135 fact sheet, the standard crew is three. The KC-135R and KC-135T normally operate with a three-person crew: a pilot, a copilot, and a boom operator. The two pilots occupy the cockpit, while the boom operator works at the rear of the aircraft, controlling the flying boom used to transfer fuel to the receiving aircraft. The National Museum of the US Air Force confirms the same crew number for the KC-135R. The more interesting question is how those three people divide the work.

The workload is substantial. The Air Force fact sheet gives the Stratotanker a maximum takeoff weight of 322,500 pounds (146,285 kg), with up to 200,000 pounds (90,719 kg) of transfer fuel and, depending on configuration, as much as 83,000 pounds (37,648 kg) of cargo. The aircraft carries all of that on a wingspan of 130 feet, 10 inches (39.88 meters), yet the normal crew is still small enough to sit around a kitchen table.

That was not always the case. Early KC-135s carried four people, with a navigator joining the two pilots and boom operator, before advances in navigation and avionics removed that position from the standard crew. The aircraft has nevertheless remained in service for decades. According to Simple Flying, the Air Force still operates roughly 396 Stratotankers across active-duty wings, the Air National Guard and the Air Force Reserve.

More recent Air Force figures cited by the Government Accountability Office put the fleet at 373 aircraft as of early March 2026, before accounting for the losses and damage sustained during Operation Epic Fury against Iran. The Congressional Research Service later listed seven KC-135s as lost or damaged during the conflict. With hundreds of Stratotankers still in the inventory and the basic crew arrangement remaining central to their operation, the obvious next question is what each crew member is actually responsible for.

The three-person crew arrangement makes more sense once the KC-135's refueling system comes into view. Aerial refueling requires two aircraft to maintain close formation while a rigid boom connects them in flight. The Air Force lists the KC-135's maximum speed at 530 miles per hour (853 km/h) at 30,000 feet (9,144 meters), although fuel transfer takes place at speeds appropriate to the aircraft involved. The receiving jet moves into position below and behind the tanker, the boom extends, and the final connection is made from the rear of the Stratotanker.

Each crew member has a specific responsibility. The pilot flies the tanker and maintains a stable flight path, while the copilot shares flying duties, handles communications and checklists, and monitors aircraft systems. At the back, the boom operator, an enlisted airman, controls the boom and guides its nozzle into the receiving aircraft. The National Museum of the US Air Force explains that the operator uses small wing-like control surfaces called ruddervators to steer the boom into position. Working from a prone position and looking through a window, the operator effectively flies the boom itself. The system can transfer nearly all the KC-135's usable fuel, while a drogue attachment can be fitted to support aircraft equipped with refueling probes. The arrangement has proved capable of some extraordinary missions.

The museum's KC-135R earned the Mackay Trophy for a sortie flown on May 31, 1967, after a Navy pilot was shot down in Southeast Asia and a rescue operation ran into fuel difficulties. Two US Navy Douglas KA-3 Skywarriors kept a pair of Vought F-8 Crusaders airborne, but both the tankers and the fighters were running low on fuel. The KC-135 crew began refueling the KA-3s while continuing to pass fuel to the F-8s. In effect, one tanker was refueling another tanker that was simultaneously refueling a fighter. The KC-135 subsequently provided additional fuel to two McDonnell Douglas F-4 Phantom fighters on its way to an alternative landing base.

Interestingly, although the KC-135 could operate with a basic crew of three, the aircraft involved in this award-winning mission carried four. Its crew consisted of Major John H. Casteel, aircraft commander; Captain Richard L. Trail, copilot; Captain Dean L. Hoar, navigator; and Master Sergeant Nathan C. Campbell, boom operator. This historical example illustrates the distinction between the aircraft's earlier four-person arrangement and its modern standard crew. The additional crew member was a navigator, not a flight engineer.

Here’s how the B-52’s crew works and why the United States Air Force wants fewer airmen.

The navigator's presence on earlier KC-135 missions helps explain how the tanker's crew evolved over time, but it also highlights a more fundamental difference between the aircraft and its civilian contemporaries: the absence of a dedicated flight engineer. The tanker was developed alongside the Boeing 707, and many airliners of the period used a third cockpit crewmember to monitor engines and systems. Yet Air Force records for the KC-135 identify pilots, a boom operator and, on earlier versions, a navigator.

The absence of a flight engineer from the standard KC-135 crew does not mean the aircraft never employed one. In a 2017 Air Force profile, Master Sgt. Robert Self was described as the service's last KC-135 flight engineer, following a career that included assignments on specialized NKC-135 and KC-135 aircraft used for testing and support programs. His responsibilities included operating the fuel panel, monitoring aircraft systems and advising the pilots. He also recalled that earlier KC-135 configurations had carried both flight engineers and navigators, positions that gradually disappeared as onboard computers and avionics became more capable.

Two pilots were always intended to occupy the front seats, with the boom operator handling refueling from the rear. Then the avionics changed. As reported by the National Guard in a story about Iowa's 185th, PACER CRAG brought compass, radar, and GPS improvements to the fleet by the early 2000s, while modern GPS removed the need for the navigator on standard missions. GlobalSecurity's overview of the program likewise notes that the commercial off-the-shelf upgrade eliminated the navigator requirement on most missions. The Simple Flying report mentioned earlier adds that digital flight decks and enhanced autopilots have further reduced the workload.

The tradeoff is workload. A base spokesman at Fairchild told the Spokane Journal that, while the upgrades were arriving,it basically meant more responsibility for the pilot and copilot. Navigation functions moved into the avionics, while some tasks previously handled by another crew member became part of the cockpit workload. This distinction is important when comparing the KC-135 with the Boeing KC-46, which was designed from the outset around a very different refueling station and a more modern approach to crew responsibilities.

The easiest way to see the difference is to look at the boom operator. On the KC-135, that person works at the rear of the aircraft and looks outside through a window. On the KC-46 Pegasus, there is no comparable window to look through. According to Air Mobility Command's KC-46A fact sheet, the Pegasus uses a fly-by-wire refueling boom and gives its Air Refueling Operator panoramic displays with wingtip-to-wingtip situational awareness. From that station, the operator controls the boom, centerline drogue, and wing aerial refueling pods.

The screen-based system was intended to offer advantages, but it also created problems that required a major redesign. The same fact sheet says that the Air Force and Boeing agreed in April 2020 on the final Remote Vision System design, known as RVS 2.0, after deficiencies had affected safe and effective refueling. The issue has not disappeared completely: as Simple Flying reported, the Pegasus still has refueling limitations with some US Air Force aircraft, including the FairchildA-10 Warthog, while Boeing works on boom and vision-system fixes. The KC-135's window may look primitive alongside the KC-46's cameras, but it also offers a remarkably direct view of the aircraft being refueled.

The contrast does not mean the KC-135 is about to disappear. According to Simple Flying, the Air Force originally planned to field 179 KC-46s, but that figure has since grown substantially. The current program calls for 263 Pegasus tankers, almost 100 more than the original requirement, as the service looks to replace much of its aging KC-135 fleet. As of early March 2026, the Air Force had 373 KC-135s and 103 KC-46As in its inventory, according to the Government Accountability Office. The Pegasus is the newer design, but the Stratotanker remains a major part of the force and is being kept in service for decades longer than originally intended. That creates an important question about the three-person crew: is it sufficient for every mission the aging tanker is now being asked to perform?

How many crew members does the V-22 Osprey need? The answer depends on the military service, the mission, and the demands of each variant.

The three-person crew is a starting point, not a fixed rule. The Air Force fact sheet notes that some missions require a navigator and that only a limited number of navigator suites are available for those specialized tasks. It is an uncommon arrangement today, but it shows why the published crew number needs a little context: the KC-135's staffing changes with the mission.

Aeromedical evacuation is the clearest example. The KC-135 can carry litter and ambulatory patients on patient support pallets, and the fact sheet says an aeromedical evacuation mission adds a basic medical crew of five: two flight nurses and three medical technicians. That number can change according to the patients being carried. In the basic configuration described by the Air Force, a hospital mission can therefore put eight crew members aboard before the patients themselves are counted.

For aeromedical evacuation, the KC-135's cargo compartment can be fitted with a stanchion litter system, allowing patients to travel on a secured litter rather than ordinary passenger seats. The system must be assembled and attached inside the aircraft by support personnel, while the medical team brings the equipment needed to monitor and care for patients during flight.

Another issue that is harder to solve with crew changes is age. The last KC-135 was delivered in 1965, so even the newest aircraft are now decades old. As reported by ExecutiveBiz, SNC has assembled a team with BAE Systems, Collins Aerospace and GE Aerospace to pursue the Air Force's KC-135 Center Console Refresh, a program aimed at replacing aging fuel-system equipment, flight displays and computing architecture. SNC announced the consortium in November 2026.

BAE would design the fuel management system to reduce pilot workload; Collins, which has supplied KC-135 avionics for more than three decades, would add new displays and computers built on an open architecture; and GE Aerospace would contribute avionics already flying on the KC-46 and Lockheed C-130 Hercules. The proposal also includes autothrottle capability, with performance projected from July 2028 through June 2038 and the award still anticipated. In other words, the same aircraft that learned to do without a navigator decades ago may soon get another set of tools designed to make the remaining crew's jobs easier.

The standard KC-135 Stratotanker crew consists of three people: a pilot, a copilot, and a boom operator. Earlier configurations commonly included a fourth crew member, a navigator, whose position gradually disappeared as navigation systems and avionics improved. Specialized missions can still require additional personnel, while aeromedical evacuation typically adds five medical crew members to the basic crew. Flight engineers also served aboard certain specialized KC-135 aircraft, but they were not part of the standard operational crew. The result is an aircraft that has retained its essential three-person operating arrangement while adapting to decades of technological change.

That makes the boom operator the most distinctive member of the crew. From the rear of the tanker, one person is responsible for the final connection between two aircraft moving in formation, doing it through a window that has been part of the KC-135's design for generations. The KC-46 approaches the same task from the opposite direction, replacing that view with cameras and displays. The basic mission has barely changed; the way the crew carries it out has.

The KC-135's story is not yet finished simply because the KC-46 is entering the force. Looking ahead, Air & Space Forces Magazine reports that the Air Force plans to keep the KC-135 until at least 2050, even as it considers a bridge tanker and a future Next-Generation Air-Refueling System. If the cockpit refresh moves forward, the old tanker could receive a substantially modernized flight deck under the program's 2028 to 2038 timeline. For a design that first flew in the 1950s, the next chapter may be less about adding people and more about giving the same three-person crew better tools for the job.

#6167. Chase Sapphire Reserve Business Bonus: 200K Points Welcome Offer

The Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ is Chase’s premium business card. While the card has a steep annual fee, it also has strong perks, and for many people, will prove to be more than worthwhile.

We’re currently seeing a highest-ever Sapphire Reserve Business bonus, which matches the best bonus we’ve seen on this card. I’d like to recap the details of the offer, including talking about eligibility, and why the card could be worth it. While this is a limited time welcome offer, the end date hasn’t been published.

Link: Learn more about the Sapphire Reserve for Business℠

The Chase Sapphire Reserve Business currently has a limited time highest-ever welcome offer of 200,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards after spending $30,000 within the first six months.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Chase Ultimate Rewards points to be worth 1.7 cents each. That means to me, the welcome bonus on this card is worth $3,400, which is incredible, among the best welcome offers out there. Admittedly the spending requirement is big (you need to average $5,000 per month in spending over six months), but so is the bonus.

For context on the Sapphire Reserve Business bonus history, when the card launched in 2025, we saw the same offer that’s currently available, for 200,000 points. Then in early 2026 we saw an offer for 150,000 points, before the offer for 200,000 points returned. Initially the offer for 200,000 points was supposed to end in September 2026, but it was extended, though we don’t know the official end date.

When it comes to applying for the Chase Sapphire Reserve Business, eligibility is unrelated to that of any other Chase Sapphire or Chase Ink card. That means if you’re eligible for business credit cards, you should be eligible for the welcome offer on this card, making this offer pretty widely available.

Keep in mind the general rules of applying for Chase cards, including the 5/24 rule, whereby you may not be approved if you’ve opened five or more new card accounts in the past 24 months (though select business cards don’t count toward that total).

If you’re trying to understand general Chase business card restrictions, the Chase Ink cards probably give you the best sense of what you can expect in terms of eligibility. You don’t need a corporation to apply for the Sapphire Reserve Business, as a sole proprietorship would qualify as well. So even a side gig (like freelancing or having a rental property) would potentially qualify you for the card.

There’s not a specific credit score you need to get approved for the Sapphire Reserve Business, though I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected, as it’s one of only many factors that goes into deciding on approvals.

The $795 annual fee Chase Sapphire Reserve Business is a pretty compelling business card. As is the case with many premium cards, the idea is that the annual fee can be justified based on a combination of the rewards structure, benefits, and airport lounge access, among other things.

The Chase Sapphire Reserve Business bonus currently offers up to 200,000 Ultimate Rewards points, which is in line with the highest ever publicly available welcome offers that we’ve seen on the card.

While the Sapphire Reserve Business has a steep annual fee, it also offers strong perks, so I’m sure many people will have no issues justifying this annual fee. Either way, if you’re eligible for the card and can complete the spending requirement, this welcome offer is incredibly tempting, and a great reason to apply for the card.

#6165. American Airlines Concierge Key: Benefits & How To Earn This Invitation-Only Status

Concierge Key is American Airlines’ invitation-only elite status. In this post, I’d like to take a close look at this elite status, and talk about what it is, how you can earn it, what the benefits are, etc. The truth is that very little is officially published about this, so we mostly have to go off of data points.

The reality is that these invitation-only elite tiers are kind of genius from the perspective of airlines. That’s because a not-insignificant portion of the frequent flyer community finds this status to be rather “sexy,” and will go out of their way to earn it. Since the qualification requirements aren’t published, it keeps people on the hamster wheel, booking as many expensive tickets as possible.

On the most basic level, Concierge Key is American’s invitation-only elite status level. There’s no published criteria to earn it, and it has to be renewed every program year, so you can earn it one year and lose it the next.

Going back many years, Concierge Key was completely separate from the AAdvantage program, but that’s no longer the case. Nowadays Concierge Key is a formal part of the AAdvantage program, and it’s a tier above Executive Platinum status (American’s highest elite tier with published qualification criteria).

I think it’s also worth mentioning that Concierge Key is perhaps the most well-known invitation-only elite status in the industry, as it was a major theme of the popular 2009 movie “Up In The Air,” starring George Clooney. Ugh, I can’t believe that was over 15 years ago.

The criteria to earn Concierge Key is not published, but generally there are a few ways to earn it.

One way is to spend a ton on American Airlines travel. We’re talking $50,000+ of spending per year. That’s not to say that spending $50,001 will get you Concierge Key status, but rather that if you spend less than that, don’t assume you have any real chance of being invited. As a matter of fact, nowadays you might need to spend significantly more than that. So you absolutely can earn Concierge Key purely through your own travel, and that’s probably the most common way it’s earned.

We don’t fully know what American looks for in this regard, though. Does the airline care purely about the dollar amount you spend, the typical fare classes you fly in (consistently full fare first class, for example), or something else? There are also some indications that the qualification criteria vary based on markets, so you have a better chance of earning it if you’re not living in a major hub city of American.

In other words, on some level it’s competitive, and you’re ranked against other travelers in similar markets. Expect that it takes more effort to earn Concierge Key if you primarily fly out of Charlotte (CLT), Dallas (DFW), or Miami (MIA), rather than out of Atlanta (ATL), Seattle (SEA), or Tampa (TPA).

Keep in mind that nowadays American Airlines elite status is based on the Loyalty Points program, so you can even earn elite status through credit card spending. So, does non-flying activity similarly count toward Concierge Key status? The reports I’ve seen suggest that it does, but you need to engage with the program a lot. For example, I’ve heard of people earning Concierge Key through credit card spending, but we’re talking about many hundreds of thousands of dollars in spending, if not over a million dollars.

You can also earn Concierge Key through the influence you have over others’ travel. Sometimes American Airlines will give Concierge Key nominations as part of a big corporate contract, or to key travel planners who have influence over a lot of others’ travel.

American Airlines is even known to comp Concierge Key to some “influencers.” For example, going back several years, YouTuber Casey Neistat was comped Concierge Key status and was really unhappy when it was taken away.

For avoidance of doubt, I’ve never been offered Concierge Key status, and I’m totally fine with that. 😉

Just for context on how these requirements compare to Executive Platinum, that requires 200,000 Loyalty Points per year. All AAdvantage members earn one Loyalty Point per dollar spent on credit cards, and Executive Platinum members earn 11x Loyalty Points per dollar spent on flights. So Executive Platinum requires $200,000 in credit card spending or around $18,200 in spending on flights.

American Concierge Key has quite a few published benefits, but some would argue the biggest benefit of the status is better “soft” treatment in the event of irregular operations.

The first thing worth understanding is that Concierge Key automatically comes with all Executive Platinum benefits. This includes everything from oneworld Emerald status, to space available first class upgrades, to complimentary Main Cabin Extra seating, to 120% bonus miles on flights, to three free checked bags, to a free drink & snack in economy, to priority services, to same day flight changes & standby.

This also includes access to the Loyalty Point Rewards program, allowing members to select additional perks, ranging from systemwide upgrades to bonus miles. Beyond that, benefits of American Concierge Key include the following:

Assistance during irregular operations is probably both potentially the most valuable perk, and also the most inconsistent one. On a good day, Concierge Key members may get proactive rebookings when flights are canceled and delayed.

American even has a fleet of cars at hubs for Concierge Key tarmac transfers, so during a short connection you may be picked up planeside and driven to your connecting flight. At the same time, there are also instances where you’ll likely be disappointed, because Concierge Key agents aren’t going to deliver 100% of the time.

If you’re looking to at least get Concierge Key levels of airport support with a particular trip, keep in mind that American offers Five Star Service, which is a paid program for more attentive service at the airport.

In the interest of being thorough, let me also mention some perks that Concierge Key used to offer, but no longer does:

American Airlines understandably hasn’t revealed how many Concierge Key members there are, so the best we can do is speculate. If I had to guess, I’d say there are somewhere between 10,000 and 20,000 Concierge Key members. To be more exact, my assumption is that the number is roughly in the middle of that range.

In 2019 there was a clue — American worked with a company to send out chocolate to Concierge Key members, and the company posted that 11,300 packages had been prepared. Now, not all Concierge Key members received this chocolate, suggesting to me that there are more members than that.

If you’re curious how other elite ranks compare, I’d guess the number of Executive Platinum members is maybe 4-5x as high as the number of Concierge Key members. Again, that’s purely speculation on my part, and with the Loyalty Points system nowadays, the number may be even higher than that.

It’s hard to say whether something like Concierge Key is “worth it.” For one, the qualification requirements aren’t even published, so how can one say whether it’s worth it when you don’t know what it will take? Second, I’d say the value of something like Concierge Key varies greatly based on the type of traveler you are.

If you’re a domestic road warrior doing 200 segments per year, you might actually get significant upside from the improved assistance during irregular operations, the Flagship Lounge access, etc. Meanwhile if you take a handful of international long haul business class trips per year, the upside will likely be very minimal — you’ll get to board first, but there’s not necessarily all that much more to it.

So I absolutely don’t think it’s worth going out of your way to try to earn something that doesn’t even have published qualification requirements. But if you earn it anyway, of course, it’s a nice thing to have!

The “big three” US carriers all have their own invitation-only elite status, with other programs including Delta 360 and United Global Services. So how do they all compare?

The reality is that all three tiers are primarily about better improved “soft” treatment, including during irregular operations. On paper, though, I’d say that Concierge Key is probably the strongest of the tiers, in terms of the number of perks, including additional lounge access to the carrier’s most premium lounges. A couple of thoughts, though:

Concierge Key is American Airlines’ invitation-only elite status. It gives you priority over Executive Platinum members for just about everything, lounge access, and also (hopefully) proactive help in the event of irregular operations. However, don’t expect it to earn it if you don’t spend at least $50,000 per year on American Airlines flights, and even then it’s not a sure bet.

Is the status life changing? While I’ve never had it, I’m inclined to say “no.” But others certainly may disagree…

If you’re a Concierge Key member (or have been one in the past), what has been your experience with the status? How does it compare to Executive Platinum status?

I was a CK for 10 years thanks to my former employer (we did a lot of long haul international travel in business class). The automatic domestic upgrades were nice, the Flagship Lounge access impressed friends and family (said one experienced traveler when we were handed champagne at the FL in ORD, "Wow, I heard stories about this but assumed it was an urban legend"), the expediters at certain international airports were helpful, and getting to the front of the lines during storms and chaotic days like today was reassuring. The most important benefit, though, was the elimination of hassles -- the tight connection, the missed flight and, in one memorable case, helping my daughter get out of Paris in the midst of a nationwide transportation strike when she wasn't even flying AA. My colleagues and I referred to the CK team as "the angels" because they could perform miracles. We often joked (sort of) that our employer could cancel our health insurance, seize our retirement benefits, but that they would have to pry our CK card out of our cold, dead hands. When I left for a new position at a much smaller company, I was able to keep my CK status for the remainder of the program year (about six months). Watching it flip to "Executive Platinum" at 12:01 am on March 1 -- yes, I stayed up to mourn -- was unnerving, but somehow I survived...

As AA evolved over the years, it wasn't a fit for me any longer. At the same time, I recognized there was an opportunity cost to sticking with AA. And, I found I could secure most of the CK benefits I received for substantially less than that opportunity cost.

As an Uber driver, I picked up a lot of United Global Services travelers. A good amount of them are telling me that some companies can purchase Global Services for their employees. No need to earn it by invite only. Of course, the companies are spending a large amount with United Airlines.

As a CK I think AA really hones in on LPs and secondary whether you fly paid premium or at least buy upgrades. If you're relying on complimentary upgrades then do not expect CK other than when AA seemingly gives CK status indiscriminately for the first year. Presumably trolling for heavier flyers that spread their flying across two or more airlines and AA would like all of or most of that business. As far as the perks, they are not always guaranteed. Sometimes there is someone at the gate to get you onboard even before PreBoards, sometimes nada. Sometimes you're meet at the gate with a representative to whisk you off to the FL or your next gate in a Cadillac Escalade. Other times again nada. The air transfers AFAIK are only available at hub airports while a representative at the gate will happen, if it does, at any airport with an AC. I do my own research and decisions during irregular operations and whether a TA or a lounge representative they're always willing to do my desired changes. Also, CKs can request a backup and guarantee seating on another flight (assuming there's open seating) if something starts to look dicey. Last April I was offered a one year extension with several options. I chose 250K miles (I have nearly 3mm miles) plus $2.5K in cash.

#6164. Richard Avedon, Fashion Guru, Does Old Age

A moving, incisive photography exhibition in Toronto and Montreal explores the way of all flesh.

Left: Richard Avedon, Gloria Swanson, actor, New York, September 4, 1980, gelatin silver print. Right: Richard Avedon, The Duke and Duchess of Windsor, Waldorf Astoria, suite 28A, New York, April 16, 1957, gelatin silver print.

© The Richard Avedon Foundation, courtesy of the Museum of Modern Art, New York, Committee on Photography Fund

Old faces — some seem to crease and crumble as we watch — were a specialty for Richard Avedon (1923–2004), the photographer famous for his fashion work for Vogue, Harper’s Bazaar, Revlon, and Elle, magazines not known for plugging geezers. I didn’t know this, so I learned something new in my first minutes in Richard Avedon Immortal: Portraits of Aging, 1951–2004, finishing its tour next month, when it goes to The Image Center in Toronto and the Montreal Museum of Fine Arts. Avedon was a pioneer in presenting cool, stark, tough beauty — he gave us a nude Nastassja Kinski with a boa constrictor licking her earlobe, Brooke Shields in jeans, and lots of movie stars and potentates at their peaks. But old age? Shades of decadence are one thing, but decrepitude?

The Image Center is Canada’s premiere photography museum and part of Toronto Metropolitan University. The exhibition there is similar to Montreal’s edition and displays 100 Avedon portraits. Avedon died more than 20 years ago, and the show spans 50 years, so the subjects are from another era. That said, old age is timeless as well as time-limited. On view are superstars such as Gloria Swanson, Ronald Reagan, the Duke and Duchess of Windsor, and the Dalai Lama. Then there are the period pieces like Dorothy Parker, Oscar Levant, Ezra Pound, and Coco Chanel.

Brian T. Allen is National Review’s art critic.

Avedon was a pioneer in presenting cool, stark, tough beauty — he gave us a nude Nastassja Kinski with a boa constrictor licking her earlobe, Brooke Shields in jeans, and lots of movie stars and potentates at their peaks. But old age? Shades of decadence are one thing, but decrepitude?

The Image Center is Canada’s premiere photography museum and part of Toronto Metropolitan University. The exhibition there is similar to Montreal’s edition and displays 100 Avedon portraits. Avedon died more than 20 years ago, and the show spans 50 years, so the subjects are from another era. That said, old age is timeless as well as time-limited. On view are superstars such as Gloria Swanson, Ronald Reagan, the Duke and Duchess of Windsor, and the Dalai Lama. Then there are the period pieces like Dorothy Parker, Oscar Levant, Ezra Pound, and Coco Chanel.

Brian T. Allen is National Review’s art critic.

#6163. Breaking: FAA Issues Nationwide Ground Stop For All US Flights

* Last Updated: 6:00 PM EST November 13, 2026 by Paul Hartley

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a rare nationwide ground stop at all US airports following communication failures affecting "multiple" air traffic control centers on Friday. Citing extraordinary circumstances and safety concerns, the FAA has suspended all departures until further notice. International arrivals will be handled individually while technicians investigate the disruption.

The exact cause of the ground stop is not yet known, but in a statement obtained by CNBC, the FAA said, "communication issues" impacted air traffic control (ATC) centers. Aviation watchdog JonNYC reported that the halt is not a “9/11 type of event”, which required flights to be forced to land at the closest airport available.

Currently, all airborne aircraft are being allowed to continue flying until further notice. According to FlightAware, more than 6,500 flights are currently halted.

"There has been a temporary telecommunications outage - out of an abundance of caution all flights have been halted. Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis."

FlightRadar24 is reporting that more than 1,000 flights had already been canceled by 6:00 PM. Cirium data indicates that more than 11,000 flights were still set to depart across the US on Friday after the ground stop was put in place, so cancellations are expected to increase significantly as the evening progresses.

Ground controllers will also face growing difficulty as aircraft continue to land and none depart, putting pressure on already stressed infrastructure and increasignly scarce gate availability.

#6161. Which Hotel Credit Cards Offer Free Night Awards, And Are They Worth It?

Hotel credit cards are among the most underrated out there. Understandably a lot of people get cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more) and Chase Sapphire Reserve® Card (learn more) to maximize the rewards they’re earning for their spending, and that’s a great idea. These cards offer valuable bonus categories, no foreign transaction fees, great travel coverage, and more.

But I think supplementing one of those cards with hotel credit cards can make a lot of sense. That’s because hotel credit cards largely offer some incredible perks that more than justify the annual fee, including free hotel elite status, and even some free night certificates. So even if you’re not loyal to a hotel group, it’s easy to get outsized value.

In this post, I’d like to specifically look at which credit cards offer free nights as part of their rewards structure, how you can earn them, and if they’re worth it.

There are hotel credit cards issued by Hilton Honors, IHG One Rewards, Marriott Bonvoy, and World of Hyatt, which offer the opportunity to earn free night awards. To be clear, I’m not talking about the ability to earn points, but instead, the ability to earn free night awards that can be redeemed at a set of properties.

These free nights come in different forms — some free night awards are offered for spending a certain amount on a card, and some free night awards are offered as an annual benefit just for having a card, with no spending required.

So let’s take a look at the details of how these free night awards work, and then we’ll talk about whether they’re worth it. Note that I’m focusing specifically on cards that offer free night awards on an ongoing basis (rather than as part of a welcome offer), and am also limiting this to cards that are open to new applicants.

Hilton Honors has two credit cards that give cardmembers the ability to earn free night awards:

Hilton Honors free night awards are my single favorite hotel free night awards out there, given that they have no category caps, and they’re valid for 12 months from when they’re issued. I value Hilton points at 0.5 cents each.

Hilton free night awards can be redeemed for standard rooms at properties costing up to 250,000 points per night, and there’s only a small list of excluded properties. They’re even valid at Small Luxury Hotels of the World (SLH) properties that are part of the Hilton Honors partnership. It’s easy to redeem these at properties costing $1,000+ per night.

IHG One Rewards has three credit cards that give cardmembers the ability to earn free night awards:

IHG One Rewards free night awards are also potentially quite valuable, and they expire 12 months from when they’re issued. I value IHG points at 0.5 cents each.

While IHG free night awards are capped at properties costing a certain number of points, what I really like is how you can top them off with an unlimited number of points. So if a hotel requires 100,000 points, you could use a 60,000 point free night certificate, and then top it off with 40,000 points.

Marriott Bonvoy has four credit cards that give cardmembers the ability to earn free night awards:

Marriott Bonvoy free night awards are also extremely lucrative, and they expire 12 months from when they’re issued. I value Marriott points at 0.7 cents each.

While Marriott free night awards are capped at properties costing a certain number of points, you can top them each off with up to 25,000 points, to redeem at more expensive properties. So you could book a hotel costing 60,000 points per night by redeeming a 35,000 point free night award, and then redeeming 25,000 additional points.

World of Hyatt Honors has one credit card that give cardmembers the ability to earn free night awards:

World of Hyatt free night awards are valuable, but definitely the most restrictive of the bunch. Free night awards issued with the card expire 12 months after they’re issued. I value World of Hyatt points at 1.4 cents each.

Category 1-4 covers a lot of Hyatt properties (these can cost up to 25,000 points per night), but the catch is that you can’t use these certificates to redeem at more expensive properties by topping them off. Still, it should be very easy to get outsized value.

I’ll let my credit card portfolio speak for itself — I have quite the selection of hotel credit cards. They’re not necessarily cards that I spend a ton on, but instead, they’re cards I largely have because of the very strong perks that they offer, which to me, more than justify the annual fee. Let me just give a few direct examples…

I have the Hilton Honors Aspire Card, and it’s my single favorite hotel credit card. The card offers a massive number of perks, but in particular, the free night alone more than justifies the annual fee for me. I try to use this at properties that would retail for $1,000+ per night, so it’s pretty awesome to get that, along with all kinds of other perks, just for having the card.

I also think there’s merit to spending $60,000 per year on the card, if you can swing it. That spending would earn you a minimum of 180,000 points (since you earn at least 3x points per dollar spent with the card), plus two additional free night awards, potentially worth up to 500,000 points. So this is a great card to consider if you’re making a big purchase.

In the case of Marriott Bonvoy, I have both the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Card and Marriott Bonvoy Business Card, which get me free night awards worth 85,000 and 35,000 points, respectively. These also in and of themselves more than justify the annual fees on the cards. I generally redeem the larger free night award for a luxury hotel stay, while I redeem the lesser free night award for a stay at a mid-range property.

Lastly, I also have the World of Hyatt Credit Card, and that free night award also more than justifies the annual fee in and of itself. Admittedly I wish the free night award cap would be increased to reflect inflation, but even so, I get a ton of value out of this. At an absolute minimum, I use it when I have an overnight near JFK to stay at the Hyatt Regency JFK, which typically costs $300+ if paying cash.

There are potentially lots of great benefits to hotel credit cards, including big welcome bonuses, easy opportunities to earn hotel status, generous rewards structures for spending, and more.

The best part is that most issuers let you have multiple credit cards, meaning you can potentially earn more than one free night certificate per year. In the case of just about all of the above cards, I’d say the free night certificates more than justify the annual fees.

What’s your favorite hotel credit card free night certificate?

#6160. Elizabeth Warren’s Plan to Abolish Credit Cards

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D., N.Y.), and Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D., Mass.) host a roundtable on housing affordability and accessibility on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., January 7, 2026.

Elizabeth Warren, never short on annoyances, thinks that interest on consumer credit cards is too high.

The average rate currently hovers around 21 percent. Her solution: Pass a law to cap interest rates at 10 percent. She says she has a bill ready to go, and like-minded lawmakers have signaled their support for controlling rates.

Like any other price ceiling, an interest cap would create a shortage of the product it attempts to make more affordable. With only a tiny fraction of credit cards now offering interest at 10 percent or less, capping rates at that level would force lenders to dramatically restrict accounts — requiring borrowers to put up collateral or limiting access to people with exceptionally good credit — or eliminate them outright.

To progressives, interest on credit cards is nothing but usury — the exploitation of poor borrowers who can’t afford to pay their bills on time. Warren’s sales pitch implies that, under her bill, people would enjoy the same credit just at a lower cost. In reality, almost everyone would see their current credit cards disappear.

Regrettably, Warren may also find allies for her proposal among Republicans. She claims she is open to working with President Trump, who called in 2024 for a temporary cap on credit card interest of “around 10 percent.” Senator Josh Hawley (R., Mo.), a right-wing progressive of sorts, recently joined hands with Bernie Sanders to translate that thoughtless musing into legislation.

Interest rates are not some arbitrary number. They are the price for lenders to provide liquidity on the promise, but never the certainty, that it will be repaid. To issue loans through a credit card, banks must first obtain the money by borrowing it themselves, either from depositors or other financial institutions. Interest must be paid on that debt and passed through to cardholders.

It’s true that rates on credit cards, as well as other consumer loans, are typically much higher than those for mortgages and businesses. That is because personal credit is one of the riskiest kinds to extend. Unlike secured loans, repayment depends wholly on borrowers’ creditworthiness. That often fails to hold up: 13 percent of credit-card balances are seriously past due, and approximately 5 percent of debt is never repaid. Higher interest rates exist to compensate for these losses.

Rates also vary based on individual creditworthiness. Borrowers with poor credit history, or people just starting to build their history after leaving childhood or moving to the country, have the most to lose from interest caps. They must accept costlier rates to obtain any credit whatsoever, and if lenders can’t adjust for their added risk, they will simply be cut off. Those in need of funds will instead have to turn to pawnshops or illegal loan sharks.

The credit card industry could always use more competition to keep interest rates at their fair market level. Ironically, the Dodd-Frank Act that Elizabeth Warren championed likely reduced the availability of consumer credit by increasing lenders’ regulatory burden. She also despises credit reporting agencies for tracking borrowers’ repayment histories, even though they replaced a far more discretionary and intrusive system in which bankers evaluated applicants’ personal reputations. For someone so appalled by alleged discrimination in finance, Warren should love objective credit reports.

By and large, Americans like their credit cards and wish to keep them. In trying to rescue consumers from their own financial decisions, Warren would deprive them of their plastic and consign them to infinitely more treacherous alternatives.
