#6158. What Amenities Make An Airport Lounge Good? Here’s My Take…

I write a lot about airport lounges on the blog, ranging all the way from domestic lounges in the United States, to the best business class lounges, to the best first class lounges. When I rank the lounges that I like the most, some readers understandably have very different takes.

I thought it would be fun to start a discussion about basic expectations of airport lounges, and what makes them exceptional.

Obviously lounge standards should differ depending on whether you’re using Priority Pass to access a lounge or are traveling in international first class, so we’ll get into more detail on that below.

Broadly speaking, what I’m looking for in a lounge is a (relatively) quiet place to sit, connect to Wi-Fi, recharge electronics, use a clean bathroom, and maybe have some water or coffee. Other things are good to have, but not something I necessarily expect.

There are also some deal killers for me when it comes to airport lounges. Personally, if a lounge is packed, I have no interest in being there, and that largely reflects that over the years, terminals have become much better places to spend time:

I figured I’d share my expectations for lounges, and I’ll break it up into three tiers of lounges (admittedly some of the lines are blurred here):

I think it’s also important to note that everyone is looking for different things in lounges:

I think the two below videos from Cathay Pacific from several years ago oh-so-beautifully sum up what makes lounges great. The commentary in the videos is almost poetic.

With that out of the way, let me share my basic expectations of various types of lounges, and admittedly these reflect my preferences and biases.

My expectations for Priority Pass lounges, airport contract lounges, airline membership lounges, and credit card lounges, are pretty simple. I’m happy if I can actually consistently get in and have a quiet place to sit. Sadly that’s not as straightforward as it may sound, with so many stories of lounges denying entry to club members, Priority Pass members, etc.

What sets a “basic” lounge apart? I’d say showers, bathrooms that are significantly nicer than in the terminals, workstations, a good food selection (ideally with hot food), good coffee, and employees who actually make you feel welcome.

Just to give some examples of lounges in this category that I consider to be exceptional:

My expectations are a bit higher for purpose-built international business class lounges. In addition to what I expect from the more “standard” lounges above, I hope that international business class lounges will have hot food, a more premium drink selection, showers, and workstations.

What sets an international business class lounge apart? I’d say a la carte dining, nap rooms, barista-made coffee drinks, and generally elevated decor.

Just to give a few examples of lounges in this category that I consider to be quite good (we’re actually pretty lucky in North America):

International first class lounges are as premium as they get, so expectations should be high. In international first class lounges I expect a la carte dining, barista-made coffee, some sort of an area to rest, a truly tranquil environment, and staff who make you feel welcome.

What sets an international first class lounge apart? Dining that’s (high-end) restaurant quality, an amazing drink selection, individual nap rooms, spa treatments, and a ground experience that extends beyond the lounge. That’s to say either tarmac transfers or an escort to the gate, and that’s no doubt an area where many airlines fall short.

I’ve reviewed the world’s top first class lounges in detail, so it’s no secret what my favorite options are the Air France La Premiere Lounge Paris and Lufthansa First Class Terminal Frankfurt.

We’re all looking for different things from airport lounges, and I think that’s totally fair. Standards should differ based on what kind of a flight you’re taking, how you access the lounge, what you’re trying to accomplish by visiting a lounge, etc.

Everyone will have a different take on which lounges are great vs. just okay, and that’s fine. While I care about tranquility and good coffee, others care about great food and drinks.

I’m curious to hear from OMAAT readers — what makes a lounge great, in your book?

We didn’t have to wait long to find out how American Airlines is shaking up its route map in Los Angeles.

Just minutes after TPG reported the carrier was planning a route announcement at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), American revealed its plans. And there’s both good and bad news for AA flyers in Southern California.

Most notably, the carrier plans to bolster its service on four routes to major U.S. cities.

It’s also bringing back a route to Colorado that it hasn’t offered in a half-decade.

Plus, American will end service to two cities from LAX.

All told, Friday's changes cover nine routes from its West Coast hub. Here's what to know.

American confirmed it’s bringing back service to Grand Junction, Colorado, for the first time in five years.

It will operate seasonal regional service from LAX between May 27 and Aug. 9 with a Bombardier CRJ700.

American last operated LAX service to Grand Junction Regional Airport (GJT) in 2021, according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium.

In 2027, this route will effectively replace American’s flight to Colorado’s Aspen/Pitkin County Airport (ASE), which will be closed next summer for construction.

American will fly its LAX-GJT route with one of its smaller CRJ-700 aircraft.

Elsewhere, American will turn to two routes it’s previously offered seasonally — and sporadically —from LAX into more regular service:

Both routes will operate with an Embraer 175 regional jet.

Starting next spring, American will also add extra daily flights from LAX to several major U.S. cities.

Denver, Las Vegas and Seattle will all get additional frequencies. Plus, American will double its daily service on one transcontinental route — from LA to Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD).

Starting in May, American will offer twice-daily Dulles service. That’ll make the IAD-LAX routes a stronger complement to AA’s cross-country Los Angeles service from nearby Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA).

American will cut ties with its LAX route to Cleveland Hopkins International Airport (CLE) effective Feb. 11.

That same day, it will also end service to Des Moines, Iowa.

This network revamp in LA comes a day after American executives said the carrier was rethinking the routes it offers at its Southern California hub.

American’s LAX service today sharply lags the flight offerings it had at the airport in 2019.

Speaking Thursday, American’s chief commercial officer, Nat Pieper, said the airline would aim to offer more flights from LAX to major U.S. cities in a push to win more L.A.-based flyers.

"We’re going to grow and we’re going to invest in the local market,” he said, speaking Thursday at the Skift Aviation Forum in New York.

That expansion, Pieper noted, will be gradual — and ramp up — as infrastructure work at LAX progresses over the next two years.

#6156. Delta Air Lines Is Already Flying The Replacement For Its Aging Airbus A319s, But American & United Don't Have One

Wikimedia Commons, Robin Guess | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, and United Airlines all operate the Airbus A319. Together, the three operate over 250 examples, using it as a core aircraft slotting above their regional jets and underneath their larger narrowbodies. However, the aircraft is also old, having debuted in 1996.

The US carriers need to replace these aircraft soon, yet two out of the three haven't ordered the Airbus A319neo, Boeing 737 MAX 7, Airbus A220, or Embraer E2. Delta Air Lines has ordered 145 Airbus A220s, split between 45 A220-100s and 100 A220-300s. The 109-seat A220-100s are much smaller than an A319-100 and are really sized closer to the airline's Boeing 717-200s.

The 130-seat A220-300s, however, are almost perfectly sized to replace the 132-seat A319-100s. The other airlines have not ordered this aircraft, nor any others to replace their A319s (as well as the 737-700 in the case of United). However, they might not need these planes to replace the A319-100.

Delta first ordered the A220 back in 2016 when the aircraft was still being sold by Bombardier as the CSeries. At the time, the CSeries was a promising plane, but orders were relatively scarce, and Bombardier was desperate to break into the US market in particular. The original order consisted of 75 CS100s (now the A220-100), and Delta received the planes at such an attractive price that it prompted Boeing to file an anti-dumping petition, which was later overturned.

Delta got an amazing price for these planes that is unlikely to be matched. The aircraft is, of course, excellent for its intended missions, but capital cost plays a huge part in the economics of acquiring and operating an aircraft type. The circumstances of the order make the A220 more compelling for Delta than it would be if American or United ordered the type simply because they would need to pay more money.

This is especially true when considering that it would come with high integration costs. Delta has experienced excellent results with the A220, and has since added 70 orders in total. While the original order solely consisted of 75 CS100s/A220-100s, all subsequent orders have been for the A319-sized A220-300.

Meanwhile, the airline has converted 30 A220-100 orders to the larger variant. While the A220-100 is a competent aircraft in its own right, the A220-300 has more seats without burning significantly more fuel, and the aircraft doesn't even have a significant range penalty for most airlines' purposes.

While the US airlines operate large fleets of last-generation small widebodies, American and United have not ordered any current-generation examples. However, this is because their replacement for the A319-100 is the A321neo and the 737 MAX 10. Both airlines have been upgauging because the A321neo and 737 MAX 10 offer significantly better per-seat economics than other narrowbody aircraft.

This makes them much more compelling to operate than their smaller counterparts. American Airlines has ordered 206 A321neos in total while also acquiring ten used examples, and it's ordered 115 737 MAX 10s. United Airlines has ordered 210 A321neos, 224 737 MAX 9s, and 167 737 MAX 10s. Both airlines have also ordered the 737 MAX 8, but in smaller numbers (103 for American and 123 for United).

What will actually happen is the new large narrowbodies will take over the carrier's highest demand routes, displacing smaller aircraft down the network and sending the A319-100s to the scrapyard. Delta has done this exact thing, ordering 100 737 MAX 10s and 189 A321neos. While it is taking new A220s, these aircraft are not necessarily replacing the A319-100s one for one.

Instead, Delta will again use its new large narrowbodies to take over its busiest routes, which will displace other aircraft, including the A220s in some cases. Meanwhile, the A319-100s will go away. For all three airlines, it's their large narrowbodies that will enable displacements throughout the network.

Over the past 15 years, Delta has ordered 145 A220s, while it also leased 88 717s from Southwest Airlines for an exceptionally low price. American Airlines ordered 32 A319-100s new from Airbus. Otherwise, all of Delta's narrowbody orders have been for the A321-200, A321neo, 737-900ER, and 737 MAX 10. American has otherwise only ordered the A321-200, A321neo, 737-800, 737 MAX 8, and 737 MAX 10.

Similarly, United has only taken the A321neo, 737-800, 737-900ER, 737 MAX 8, and 737 MAX 9, while holding orders for the MAX 10. There has been a noticeable trend of US airlines favoring larger narrowbodies, and even the mid-size 737-800s and 737 MAX 8s have fallen out of favor.

These aircraft simply deliver superior economics to the shrinks in their families, as the added fuel burn is far outweighed by their increased revenue potential. The tradeoff is shorter range and runway performance, but only a handful of mainline stations have truly challenging conditions. At the same time, the A320neo and 737 MAX families have solved the performance and range issues.

Across the board, US airlines are upgauging, switching to larger aircraft for short-haul flights. In the past, another reason why airlines would buy smaller aircraft is to right-size capacity, but the US legacy carriers have strongly employed fare segmentation as a core commercial strategy.

This has reduced the need to operate smaller narrowbodies, since releasing various numbers of differently priced tickets can help fill planes on slower days. This is something that United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby has publicly commented on.

Fare segmentation and basic economy fares mean that his airline no longer requires a small narrowbody to meet demand, allowing United to standardize on larger, more economical aircraft. Tellingly, United ordered 45 737-700s in 2016, added another 20 units, then converted all orders to the 737-800 and 737 MAX 9 later the same year.

American Airlines ordered 32 A319-100s new from Airbus, while also acquiring a handful of used examples. United Airlines converted all of its later 737-700 orders to larger variants, while also acquiring a handful of used A319-100s. Delta, on the other hand, ordered 145 A220s while also acquiring 88 717s. Of course, the capital costs play a huge role in this.

Specifically, the 717s were essentially a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity due to Southwest's acquisition of AirTran, which originally owned the planes, while the A220s were sold at very low prices. However, another benefit of the small narrowbodies to Delta comes from its pilot agreement.

The agreement stipulates scope clauses, which place limits and restrictions on regional jet flying contracted out to other airlines under the Delta Connection brand. The largest planes that may be flown for Delta Connection are 76-seaters, and there are hard limits on how many of these planes Delta may operate under the Delta Connection, as they are more economical than 70-seaters or 50-seaters.

Delta's scope agreement, however, allows the airline to add additional 76-seaters if it adds a new small mainline narrowbody. The 717s, in addition to being cheap to acquire, unlocked additional 76-seaters for the Delta Connection brand. The A220 order did the same thing, and this is a significant benefit given the scale of the regional operations run by the US airlines. However, this was also a very specific set of circumstances that, combined, made the two purchases work for Delta.

These airlines are the world's three largest operators of the type.

An opportunity like the 88 717s that Southwest was looking to offload rapidly was only going to occur once, as is also the case for the pricing on Delta's initial A220 order. Beyond this, American Airlines specifically does not have a trigger in its scope clauses for additional 76-seaters if it acquires a new small narrowbody type. Rather, the size of the 76-seater fleet is tied directly to the airline's overall mainline fleet size.

For American, the aircraft has to have merit on its own, and that's difficult to justify. United Airlines does have the same trigger clause as Delta, which means that acquiring an aircraft type sized like the A319-100 would unlock additional 76-seaters. However, the carrier is currently focused on substantial network-wide growth through frequency increases and upgauging.

Buying 100+ A220s does not fit its general strategy today, especially considering United's current order book, which is dominated by larger aircraft variants. For both airlines, there is less benefit to acquiring the A220 or a similar small narrowbody aircraft type like Delta has.

Apart from the unique circumstances that made the 717s and A220s attractive to Delta, however, the Atlanta-based carrier is also practicing upgauging and is noticeably doing so throughout the network. The carrier has also shied away from the 737 MAX 8, and there's a distinct possibility that it may simply not order this variant at all.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

Definitely would be cool to see an A220-300 in UA colors, but I honestly wonder if they won’t order a replacement due to their preference for larger aircraft.

#6154. The Fight Over Obamacare’s Phantom Enrollees

The Trump administration is right to take on the problem of improper enrollment.

Administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Dr. Mehmet Oz speaks during a press conference on anti-fraud initiatives at the White House campus in Washington, D.C., September 22, 2026.

More than a dozen Democratic senators are criticizing the Trump administration’s efforts to address the problem of phantom enrollments in Obamacare. In a letter to insurers, the senators accuse the companies of “colluding” with the administration to terminate coverage for more than 760,000 enrollees. Their criticism gets insurers’ financial incentives backward and overlooks the extensive safeguards the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) employed before terminating these highly suspicious enrollments.

Insurers have little incentive to drop phantom enrollees. For years, insurers have been the biggest beneficiaries of the expanded Obamacare subsidies — reaping tens of billions of dollars in higher subsidies. By making millions of plans free to consumers, Democrats created powerful incentives for improper and phantom enrollment. Given these incentives, the administration was right to scrutinize suspicious enrollments.

Brian Blase is the president of the Paragon Health Institute. He was special assistant to the president for economic policy at the White House’s National Economic Council, 2017–19.

Some of the most aspirational business-class award redemptions are increasingly hard to find, even for the most experienced points and miles enthusiasts.

Cathay Pacific is a prime example. It's harder and harder to find award availability in the Hong Kong-based airline's premium cabins, especially with partners.

But one trick still works: Look for award availability when airlines launch new routes or bring back old ones.

I was able to fly from Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) to Hong Kong International Airport (HKG) for just 75,000 Atmos Rewards points. That is a screaming deal. But there was only saver-level availability for a limited time when the schedule was first loaded.

It turned out to be a fantastic redemption, with excellent service, delicious food and a comfortable lie-flat seat for the long journey across the Pacific.

I'll have more details later in this story on how to find some of these incredible deals in business class, but first, let's talk a bit more about this flight.

Here's what my experience was like aboard Cathay Pacific's Airbus A350-900 and how you can use a similar strategy to find these elusive business-class awards.

Cathay Pacific relaunched its service to Hong Kong from Seattle in March 2026, after suspending the route during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The route originally launched in March 2019 and was canceled in November of the following year. The airline's CEO told TPG that the carrier had always wanted to restore the route, which was Seattle's first nonstop service to Hong Kong since the pandemic.

The plane was a nine-year-old A350-900 with the ship number B-LRL, with 38 business-class seats, 28 premium economy seats and 214 economy seats.

It was a very comfortable way to cross the Pacific and opens up fun new ways to get to Asia from the U.S. West Coast. It also adds another way to use points and miles to fly to Hong Kong, though as you'll read below, it's no easy task to find the lowest-level award availability.

Business-class guests on Cathay Pacific are invited to use The Club at Seattle in the South Satellite area, which is connected to the main terminal by an underground train.

The Club SEA is an independent lounge that participates in Priority Pass. It offers a buffet of hot and cold food items and free drinks. It's basic, and it doesn't hold a candle to Cathay Pacific's own lounges in places like San Francisco and Hong Kong (no noodle bar here). However, it will do the trick for a quick drink and bite.

It was crowded during my quick visit, and I didn't spend much time at this lounge, since I'd had access to the beautiful Alaska Airlines lounge in the N Concourse. I grabbed a bite there before heading to the S Concourse, which is about to get a major, modern $2.5 billion renovation. It should be a much nicer place to hang out once the renovations are done.

Cathay Pacific has 38 business-class seats, split between two cabins. I was in the forward cabin with 30 seats arranged in a 1-2-1 configuration. There is a smaller cabin with just eight business-class seats behind a small galley/boarding area, which looked like a good option for a more intimate experience.

The seats fold down to 75 inches in length to become fully flat beds, though the footwell is a bit narrow.

Cathay Pacific gave out British lifestyle brand Bamford amenity kits that had moisturizer, cooling body gel, pillow mist, an eye mask, earplugs, a toothbrush and toothpaste and mouthwash. There were also noise-canceling headphones and a bottle of water at the seat.

The seat had lots of little storage areas, along with slippers (but no pajamas, as Cathay only has pajamas on select planes with first class).

Bathrooms are plentiful, with two in the front of the main business-class cabin and one more behind. The coolest thing was that the two bathrooms in front have windows — something you don't see that often on airplanes. Amenities were provided by Bamford and included a moisturizing spray and lotion.

The inflight entertainment was great, with an 18.5-inch HD touchscreen and plenty of movies and entertainment. I was able to choose from hundreds of movies and television shows (including a documentary on Cathay Pacific's 80th anniversary). There was also a tail camera and a moving map. A handheld controller is available to navigate the screen.

Cathay Pacific provides free Wi-Fi for business-class passengers, and I found it worked well on my flight. It's not as fast as Starlink, but it was still easy for me to get some work done.

I really like Cathay Pacific's business-class seats on these planes, though I'm excited to try one of Cathay's newer Aria Suite business-class products someday. Those suites are currently being installed on their Boeing 777-300ER fleet.

I'm especially hoping to see it on flights to and from John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), which the airline has hinted could come as soon as next year. (The timing of that rollout remains to be confirmed.)

A friendly and attentive crew, delicious food and good bedding made for a great flight across the Pacific. I had especially good service with flight attendants Mei, Amanda and Elsa, all of whom were super friendly and chatty.

Service wasn't as formal as some Asian airlines I've flown, and the crew was fun to be around.

A predeparture beverage of orange juice or water was served during boarding.

Not long after takeoff, flight attendants served drinks. I went with a nonalcoholic Cathay Delight, the airline's signature nonalcoholic drink, made with kiwi, coconut and mint.

That was followed by a lovely amuse-bouche of a deviled egg. I could have happily eaten 20 of them.

The egg dish was served with a Betsy Free, Cathay Pacific's nonalcoholic version of its signature Betsy beer, in a vintage-style Cathay Pacific beer can.

That was followed by an absolutely delicious lunch: a roast carrot soup with a selection of breads, a hearty buffalo mozzarella and rocket pesto salad with grilled radicchio and toasted hazelnuts, and a roasted chicken breast in a maple-chipotle barbecue sauce, served with corn on the cob, creamed spinach and garlic mashed potatoes.

The dessert cart was filled with things like cheese and fruit plates, a yogurt panna cotta, ice cream, or a raspberry tiramisu and, of course, port or wine.

The flight attendants saw me snapping a ton of pictures, so they ended up letting me sample a little bit of almost everything. What a feast!

As if that weren't enough, flight attendants later brought around a chocolate sampler.

There were also snacks set out in the area between the two business-class cabins.

I was able to pre-select a second meal before the flight, and went with a classic beef burger.

There was a nice set of options available on the pre-order menu.

That meal was served after I'd gotten a few hours of shut-eye. Cathay Pacific is well-known for its burgers, and this one didn't disappoint.

I'm not sure how they managed to make a burger served at 30,000 feet taste good, but they did.

The flight attendants helped make my bed with a Bamford-branded mattress pad, duvet and large pillow. I managed to get about five hours of sleep — not too bad.

Before landing, there was yet another meal.

Breakfast was a more traditional Chinese meal of congee with shrimp dumplings and siu mai. Honestly, at that point, I was so full that I didn't eat much of it, but I did enjoy about four cappuccinos.

I'll tell you one thing: Come hungry when flying international on Cathay Pacific.

I was able to score that business-class seat on Cathay Pacific's newly resumed flight to Hong Kong for just 75,000 Atmos Rewards points and $5.60 in federal security tax. You can also book Cathay flights with American Airlines AAdvantage miles.

Unfortunately, low-level award space has been increasingly hard to come by using partners lately. That's why I always look when a new or newly resumed route goes on sale. I've often found low-level awards when the route first comes up for booking.

That also happened recently when American Airlines announced new service to Prague and newly resumed flights to Budapest,. The airline made business-class redemptions widely available for just 55,000 Alaska Atmos Rewards points.

So when a new route starts or resumes, check award availability as soon as the seats go on sale.

Related: 9 flight award booking hacks every traveler should know

Of course, you'll likely find more availability using Cathay Pacific's own program: Asia Miles. Cathay Pacific often releases more award availability to its own members. You can transfer miles 1:1 from multiple Cathay Pacific banking partners — including Bilt and Citi ThankYou Rewards, among others — directly to Asia Miles. American Express Membership Rewards also transfers to Asia Miles but at a reduced 5:4 ratio.

Award search tools are increasingly a big part of my deal hunt. Some of my favorites include Seats.aero, ExpertFlyer (owned by TPG parent company, Red Ventures) and Roame.travel. I also rely on the Points Path award tool, which runs in my browser, so I can see award availability when I search on Google Flights.

Flexibility is another key to finding award availability like this. You'll often need to travel whenever a seat is available, not on a specific date. If you're open to multiple destinations, you'll also have better luck finding the cheapest awards, especially to destinations like Asia. Consider using wherever you find the best redemption as a jumping-off point to see other destinations in the region.

Business class on Cathay Pacific's A350-900s may not have all the excitement of its newer Aria Suite, but it's still a super-compelling product, as my recent flight from Seattle to Hong Kong showed. This trip proved once again why Cathay Pacific is one of my favorite airlines, and the newly resumed service from Seattle adds another option for American travelers.

Friendly service, a great seat, and incredible food and beverages made this trip one to remember. The best part was getting all that for just 75,000 Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards points.

Keep an eye out for newly launched (or relaunched) routes when you are looking for your next great redemption. You might get a happy surprise.

#6150. How To Redeem World Of Hyatt Points For Best Value, Maximize Award Chart

I write a lot about the value of hotel loyalty programs, and in this post, I’d like to talk about World of Hyatt. What are the best ways to redeem World of Hyatt points, how many points do you need for a free night redemption, how does the award chart work, etc.?

Let’s start by talking about the basics of redeeming World of Hyatt points — how much should you expect to pay for free nights, are there blackout dates, how much are World of Hyatt points worth, etc.?

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider World of Hyatt points to be worth 1.4 cents each. There’s no science to that, but rather I think that’s a fair, conservative valuation for what the points are worth. In other words, I won’t redeem points for a hotel stay with Hyatt unless I’m getting well over 1.4 cents of value per point (and that has to factor in the points I’m forgoing by redeeming rather than paying cash, etc.).

It’s important to come up with a points valuation for yourself (it can be different than mine), so that you can decide whether to pay cash or redeem points for a hotel stay.

I have lowered this valuation a little recently, in light of the World of Hyatt award chart devaluation we’ve seen, where Hyatt has gone from three tiers of pricing within each category to five.

World of Hyatt has no blackout dates, which is to say that if a standard room is available for sale with cash, it can also be booked with points.

Now, the important thing to keep in mind is that some hotels have a very small pool of “standard” rooms, and a vast majority of rooms at a hotel may be considered “premium.” If a hotel has 150 rooms, it’s possible that only 10 rooms are considered “standard,” so that’s the major issue you’ll run into when redeeming points at some properties.

Unfortunately in the hotel industry overall, we’ve seen a reduction in the number of standard rooms at many properties that are popular for redemptions, which is essentially a way for hotels to create indirect capacity controls.

Keep in mind that Hyatt has a great points availability calendar, which at least makes it easy to find the nights that are available with points, for those properties that are challenging.

Hopefully this isn’t an issue anyone runs into, but just keep in mind the World of Hyatt points expiration policy. World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of inactivity. Any points earning or redemption activity resets the expiration of your points by a further 24 months.

Unlike Hilton Honors, IHG One Rewards, and Marriott Bonvoy, World of Hyatt continues to publish award charts for award redemptions (the exception is Mr & Mrs Smith properties, which I’ll talk more about in a bit).

The catch is that at this point, World of Hyatt has five tiers of award pricing for standard room redemptions — Lowest, Low, Moderate, Upper, and Top — and the variance within each category is huge. So while I appreciate that there’s not technically dynamic pricing, when a Category 1 hotel can cost 3,000 or 9,000 points, and a Category 8 hotel can cost 35,000 or 75,000 points, you’re not exactly getting a lot of assurance.

The standard award chart applies at a vast majority of properties globally, including most Hyatt branded properties. There are eight categories of hotels, and 40 different pricing tiers, given the five pricing bands within each tier. Pricing ranges from 3,000 points for a Category 1 property during the “Lowest” period, and 75,000 points for a Category 8 property during the “Top” period.

Next, World of Hyatt has an all-inclusive award chart, which applies to an ever-growing number of properties across Hyatt’s all-inclusive brands. Hotels fall into one of six categories, with the similar five bands of pricing, all based on double occupancy. Pricing ranges from 12,000 points for a Category A property during the “Lowest” period, to 85,000 points for a Category F property during the “Top” period.

Lastly, World of Hyatt has an award chart for Miraval properties, which are Hyatt’s super-luxurious wellness resorts. Pricing varies based on single or double occupancy, and then there’s also the five bands of pricing.

Note that unlike Hilton Honors and Marriott Bonvoy, World of Hyatt doesn’t offer a fifth night free on award redemptions. So you’ll pay the points that correspond to the number of nights you’re staying.

World of Hyatt is the only major hotel loyalty program that lets you efficiently redeem your points for suites. This can come in the form of free night redemptions, or in the form of an upgrade award. Unlike with standard room availability, there are capacity controls on suite redemptions, so these won’t always be available just because a suite is for sale.

You can find the standard suite award chart below, for the same Category 1-8 properties as above. As you can tell, the premium for a standard suite can range from around 20% to 100%, so there’s quite a bit of variance here. In many situations this could represent a good deal. Of course the ways that hotels choose to designate suites differs by property, so in some cases this can represent a huge upgrade, while in other cases it doesn’t.

You can find the premium suite award chart below, for the same Category 1-8 properties as above. As you can tell, there’s also quite a bit of variance here in terms of how much of a premium you’re paying.

World of Hyatt also lets you upgrade to club rooms, suites, and premium suites, using points. You can find the chart for that below, though note that this is only possible when booking a fully paid stay at the flexible rate directly with Hyatt. This requires a rate code, so it’s not even combinable with Hyatt Privé rates.

There are also more capacity controls here than you’d have if redeeming Hyatt suite upgrade awards, which are issued through the Milestone Rewards program.

World of Hyatt offers Points + Cash awards, whereby you can book a stay at a hotel using a combination of points and cash. This might sound appealing to those who want to reduce the cash cost of a stay using points, or those who don’t have quite enough points for a stay.

Points + Cash redemptions follow an award chart. The way this works, you can redeem 50% of the standard points required, plus you’ll receive around 50% off the cash component of a stay, in comparison to the flexible rate.

It’s always worth taking a look at this, though more often than not I don’t find this to be as good of a deal as just outright redeeming points. Also note that Points + Cash redemptions have capacity controls, unlike free night redemptions.

Hyatt acquired luxury travel company Mr & Mrs Smith, and you’ll find that many Mr & Mrs Smith properties are bookable through Hyatt channels. This is an opportunity to earn and redeem Hyatt points for stays at all kinds of independent luxury properties that you’d not otherwise have access to with a major loyalty program.

While the opportunity to earn points is potentially exciting, the catch is that points redemptions largely represent a bad value. Award pricing is fully dynamic, and you’ll find that in many cases, points only get you around a cent each toward a stay. That’s significantly less than I value them, so I wouldn’t recommend redeeming that way.

While I wouldn’t say it’s my favorite use of points, World of Hyatt offers Dining & Spa awards, whereby you can redeem points toward a folio credit that can be applied to on-property dining and spa awards. With this, you’ll get anywhere from 1.0 to 1.54 cents of value per point.

While there are some restrictions to be aware of, this is still something that has the potential to be useful for those with lots of points, who are looking to splurge on incidentals during a stay.

With the Milestone Rewards program, World of Hyatt members can earn Guest of Honor certificates. This extends World of Hyatt Globalist status benefits over the course of a stay, for up to seven nights. These can be applied to any eligible revenue stay or points stay, and offer lots of value.

Those booked with a Guest of Honor certificate receive the standard Globalist perks, including complimentary breakfast, suite upgrades subject to availability, and much more. This is one of my favorite loyalty perks out there.

World of Hyatt has a generous policy when it comes to letting members transfer or combine points between accounts. World of Hyatt members can transfer points between accounts at a 1:1 ratio.

Members can transfer a minimum of 1,000 points, and can transfer in increments of 500 points above that. Members can transfer up to 525,000 points per transaction, and may transfer or receive up to that many points across accounts per calendar year. World of Hyatt accounts must be at least 60 days old in order to send or receive points.

World of Hyatt members are also limited to making one free points transfer every calendar month, and six free points transfers every calendar year. Transfers generally happen within 24 hours, but in rare cases could require additional review, and could take up to 10 business days.

This can be a great way to combine points in order to have enough for a particular redemption, or even to transfer points in order to make a booking out of an elite member’s account, or using a Guest of Honor award.

Nowadays many properties charge resort fees or destination fees, which are essentially a money-grab. All World of Hyatt members don’t have to pay these when redeeming points, which can add significant value. Furthermore, World of Hyatt Globalist members don’t have to pay these even on revenue stays.

As a further perk, World of Hyatt Globalist members don’t have to pay for parking on award stays (however, non-Globalist members do have to pay for parking).

World of Hyatt has three elite tiers — Discoverist (10 elite nights), Explorist (30 elite nights), and Globalist (60 elite nights). While status isn’t quite as easy to earn as with some other hotel groups, there are still some opportunities to earn status with credit cards. World of Hyatt’s co-branded credit cards include the World of Hyatt Credit Card (learn more) and World of Hyatt Business Credit Card (learn more). You can earn elite qualifying nights and status with these cards:

Even if you’re not a Hyatt loyalist, the great news is that earning World of Hyatt points is pretty easy. However, the ratios aren’t as consistently good as in the past.

In addition to being able to earn World of Hyatt points with the World of Hyatt Credit Card and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card, you can also transfer points from both Bilt Rewards and Chase Ultimate Rewards:

On top of that, World of Hyatt frequently has promotions for purchasing points. The reason this matters is because there are lots of situations where you could get outsized value simply by buying points from Hyatt and then immediately redeeming them for a hotel stay.

With the above basics out of the way about redeeming World of Hyatt points, how do you get the most value with your points? Let me share my approach to redeeming Hyatt points.

As a Hyatt Globalist member, I exclusively redeem my points for free night award redemptions in standard rooms. While I think there can be value in redeeming points for standard or premium suites, my general strategy is to redeem for standard rooms, and then use suite upgrade awards to confirm suites.

The reality is that I get huge value with my World of Hyatt points throughout the award chart, and not just at aspirational properties. Generally I decide to redeem points if I’m getting at least two cents of value per World of Hyatt point. There are several things I factor into that, though. When deciding whether to redeem points:

With World of Hyatt charging such vastly different amounts across the five bands of pricing, in some cases you’ll get the most value per point when redeeming during an off-peak period, while in other cases you’ll get the most value when redeeming during a peak period. You of course always want to compare the cash rates to the points redemption rates.

With a little bit of effort, I have no issues redeeming a vast majority of my Hyatt points for well over two cents each, in comparison to the cash cost.

Ultimately the reason I collect airline miles and hotel points is for aspirational redemptions. I try to redeem for things that I typically wouldn’t pay for in cash, where I’m getting outsized value.

So just as airline miles are best redeemed for first & business class travel, hotel points are often best redeemed for five-star properties that would cost a lot in cash. So the main reason I earn Hyatt points is to be able to redeem at properties belonging to brands like Alila and Park Hyatt. From Alila Napa Valley, to Alila Ventana Big Sur, to Alila Jabal Akhdar, to Park Hyatt Kyoto, to Park Hyatt Milan, to Park Hyatt Paris, I’ve had some amazing award redemptions over the years.

World of Hyatt is my all-around favorite hotel loyalty program. I greatly value the elite perks I receive as a Globalist member, and I also consistently get great value with my points, especially for aspirational properties. I also love how World of Hyatt points can efficiently be transferred from Chase Ultimate Rewards, providing an easy pathway to racking up this currency.

Personally my favorite use of World of Hyatt points is for stays at Hyatt’s top luxury hotels, where you’ll almost consistently get the best value, assuming you can find award availability. However, I’ve gotten great value at lower end properties as well.

Now, in fairness, the value of Hyatt points is definitely decreasing a bit at the moment, and on top of that, the reduced transfer ratio from other currencies is frustrating, and definitely eats into the value a bit. That being said, that’s true of the industry at large, as we’ve also seen endless devaluations with Hilton Honors and Marriott Bonvoy. I do still get the most value with Hyatt.

What has your experience been with redeeming World of Hyatt points?

#6149. Is It True That The Airbus A321XLR Flies With Its Nose Pitched Up At Cruising Altitude?

Did you feel like your plane was a little nose-up on your last long flight? Well, you're not wrong. In fact, nearly every single commercial jetliner cruises with a noticeable nose-high pitch for most of the journey. The physics of flight dictate that an aircraft on a steady level cruise rarely maintains a perfectly parallel relationship with the horizon. It's especially remarkable on Airbus' newest long-haul narrowbody, the A321XLR.

While a nose-up attitude is basic physics, a couple of factors make it highly noticeable on the A321XLR. An aircraft wing does not generate lift when aligned perfectly flat with the oncoming air mass. It requires a pitch of two to three degrees above the horizon to force the air under the wings and produce efficient lift. The A321 is a very long narrowbody aircraft, and its silhouette creates a clear visual profile compared to shorter aircraft like the A319.

This is not an abnormality of the A321XLR design. It is the standard operating condition for the entire commercial fleet, ranging from the small Airbus A220 to the massive Boeing 777. As a flight progresses and the engines burn through fuel, the plane becomes lighter. When it needs less lift, the fly-by-wire system gradually lowers the nose. The cabin floor is rarely level, though the tilt is subtle enough that most passengers won't notice it while seated.

Despite carrying far more weight than other planes in its class, the XLR retains the Airbus A321's baseline wingspan of 117 feet (35.8 meters). Given the restricted wing area compared to a widebody jet that flies similar routes as the XLR, it must fly at a higher angle of attack than many commercial jets. Raising the nose one to two degrees above most other airliners allows the XLR to generate more lift at a similar altitude and airspeed.

It must take off with a far greater payload than the standard A321neo, which is often configured with a higher seating capacity, because of the fuel it carries to make long journeys. That requires gradual step climbs with the XLR slowly raising and lowering its altitude relative to the fuel in its tanks as the route progresses.

Pilots on simulator forums online cite pitch ranges between one and three degrees for cruise flight. These values fluctuate depending on the precise fuel load, passenger count, and chosen speed schedule. Weight is the primary driver of these fluctuations. For the Airbus A321XLR, this calculation is pushed to the absolute extreme of the single-aisle category. The jet stands out as the heaviest iteration of the A321 family, boasting a maximum takeoff weight reaching 223,000 pounds (101,100 kg).

When heavily loaded with fuel at takeoff, the thin air at high altitudes cannot provide enough density to support an XLR efficiently. To avoid an unfavorable flight profile, the XLR is heavily reliant on step climbs. It will initially level off at a lower altitude where the air is denser. Even at this lower altitude, the engines must operate at high thrust to maintain cruise speed while holding a high nose pitch.

United’s first Airbus A321XLR begins a new premium narrowbody era for long-haul flying.

Walking toward the front of the A321XLR cabin on a transatlantic flight might make a passenger feel as though they are moving up a shallow ramp. While the plane behaves flawlessly from an engineering standpoint, its high nose-up posture changes how passengers experience the flight. That is most noticeable during the initial hours of a transcontinental mission when the aircraft is heaviest.

In the early phase of such a trip, flight attendants must manage heavy galley carts on a tilted floor. Service typically starts from the front of the cabin and moves backward, allowing the crew to push the heavy carts downhill rather than fighting gravity to push them forward. To guarantee a pleasant ride for a full passenger payload, the aircraft relies on a highly optimized, non-emergency 'comfort envelope.'

To prevent passengers from feeling any sudden jerks or wallowing motions, the autopilot performs continuous micro-trimming. The computers maintain a specific cruise speed, typically Mach 0.78, at an altitude where the air density allows the plane to ride smoothly. By keeping the XLR in the 'buffet margin' performance band, the system ensures a rock-solid, vibration-free ride for the customers in the back.

The story behind Delta's reluctance to invest in long-haul narrowbodies.

Inside the advanced cockpit of the A321XLR, a suite of flight computers handles most of the workload required to balance the jet's pitch. The flight computers eliminate the need for pilots to manually adjust the plane's controls as the trip progresses. These avionics let the flight crew spend more time focused on navigation rather than constantly correcting the aircraft's attitude.

Flying at a nose-up angle naturally creates extra aerodynamic drag. To combat this, the computer systems linking the navigation data and the engine throttles work together seamlessly. The autopilot uses a continuous feedback loop that monitors how the aircraft is interacting with the thin air. As the plane burns off fuel and changes mass, the computer automatically commands the tail stabilizers to pivot by microdegrees.

This smooth, automated adjustment gently lowers the nose to a flatter angle without requiring any input from the flight crew. The system calculates the exact engine thrust needed to glide efficiently at the ideal angle. It maintains a steady cruise speed without burning excess fuel, keeping the plane at the mathematically perfect intersection of pitch, speed, and fuel efficiency.

Analyzing the real world performance of the world's longest range narrowbody.

The A321XLR navigation computer removes all the guesswork from changing altitudes during long-haul flights. The plane cannot safely cruise at its final high altitude right after takeoff because the air is too thin to support it. The automation constantly runs real-time calculations to find the optimal moments to climb. Simultaneously, flying a long-range narrowbody like the XLR near its performance margins also requires strict safety boundaries.

When the plane reaches an ideal state, the system notifies the crew, executes the climb smoothly, and automatically recalibrates the nose position for the new altitude. The flight control software also includes hard-coded safety protections that act as an invisible safety net. If severe turbulence or a sudden wind shift tries to force the nose into a dangerously high angle, the computer automatically intervenes. It overrides unsafe tendencies and stabilizes the plane well before it approaches an aerodynamic stall.

How carriers around the world are filling the jumbo-sized void left by an icon of aviation.

The automation on the A321XLR acts as both an active stabilizer during rough weather and an immediate backup to the autopilot. The flight computers do not just wait for the plane to get bounced around. Instead, they use a real-time response system. The throttle computer continuously tracks wind shear to detect if a sudden draft causes a drop in speed. Then, the engines instantly spool up to add energy, and if a gust spikes the speed, the throttles dial back.

Accelerometers and sensors throughout the fuselage detect sudden pockets of rising or sinking air instantly. By minutely deflecting these wing surfaces in direct opposition to the bumpy air, the plane counteracts the turbulent forces. Even if the autopilot is hand-flying or navigating severe weather, the computer software enforces strict performance limits. If an extreme event exceeds the autopilot's limits, the XLR will drop offline to hand control back to the pilots.

Because an unexpected disconnection is highly critical, the cockpit is designed to make the handover impossible to miss. The plane will not allow the nose to point higher than 30 degrees up or lower than 15 degrees down, and the system limits the maximum roll angle to 67 degrees. If the autopilot projects that intervention is needed to stay within tolerances, red flashing warning lights illuminate directly in front of both pilots on the main dashboard panels.

The evolving industry, and climbing price, of extra-large turbofan engine repairs.

Although the A321XLR looks identical to a standard variant of the family, the jet has some subtle differences inside and out to match the flight efficiency of its light, shorter-haul peers. Lighter, standard A321neo jets are optimized for high-capacity, short-haul routes where low-speed lift during frequent takeoffs and landings is a major priority. To achieve this, standard A321s have featured complex, heavy double-slotted inboard flaps. For the A321XLR, Airbus deleted the double-slotted configuration in favor of a single-slotted inboard flap.

The simpler control surface slashes the wing's physical weight and provides an optimized profile that reduces drag in high-altitude cruise. During an 11-hour long-haul cruise, a double-slotted mechanism creates excessive, unnecessary weight and parasitic aerodynamic drag. To ensure the plane doesn't lose low-speed lift during takeoff at maximum weight, Airbus pairs this single-slotted flap with advanced software that introduces automated flap programming.

Looking at the internal components, the XLR once again differs from older long-range models like the A321LR. On the legacy jets, extra fuel is carried in up to three separate additional center tanks which resemble large cargo containers bolted into the luggage hold. These add weight and eat up cargo space that would otherwise be used for bags and shipments. The XLR solves this by replacing separate cargo-bay tanks with a single, permanent rear center tank.

Concentrating thousands of liters of fuel entirely behind the wings completely shifts the aircraft’s weight and balance. As the flight progresses and the aft tank drains, the center of gravity dynamically sweeps forward. The XLR's flight computers use automated fuel management to precisely monitor fuel burn across the outer wings, forward tanks, and rear tank, keeping the plane perfectly balanced in its optimal cruise pitch from takeoff to touchdown.

#6148. An Intellectual History of California’s Proposition 40

How a French academic research project and an elite public university nearly took down the Golden State’s venture capital economy with a wealth tax

People attend a rally in support of Proposition 40 and in opposition to Propositions 41 and 42 ahead of the midterm elections in Los Angeles, Calif., October 5, 2026.

On November 3, California voters narrowly rejected Proposition 40, a 5 percent tax on the net worth of the state’s billionaires. That outcome was not assured. In September, the measure led 52 percent to 46 percent in the Public Policy Institute of California’s survey of likely voters. Had it passed, the state that received 62 percent of all U.S. venture capital dollars in 2025 would have begun taxing founders on the paper value of companies, potentially driving them elsewhere.

The union that sponsored Proposition 40, SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, supplied the signatures and most of the campaign money. The idea came from an intellectual movement that began with the French economist Thomas Piketty, found an institutional home at the University of California, Berkeley, and received financing from the foundation of a Boston insurance executive.

People attend a rally in support of Proposition 40 and in opposition to Propositions 41 and 42 ahead of the midterm elections in Los Angeles, Calif., October 5, 2026.

Marc Joffe is a fellow at the California Policy Center.

#6146. FAA Issues Nationwide Ground Stop, Shuts Down The Skies: What’s Going On?

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a nationwide ground stop, which is pretty unprecedented. Admittedly we’ve had our fair share of air traffic control issues in the United States over the years. But this is really on a different level, unlike anything we’ve seen since 9/11, in terms of operational disruptions. I guess it’s fitting that this is happening on Friday the 13th.

At 3:54PM ET today (Friday, November 13, 2026), the FAA issued a ground stop for flights across the country, as pilots received the following message:

DUE TO EXTRAORDINARY CIRCUMSTANCES AND FOR REASONS OF SAFETY. ATTENTION ALL AIRCRAFT OPERATORS, BY ORDER OF THE FEDERAL AVIATION COMMAND CENTER ALL AIRPORTS ARE GROUND STOPPED. ALL DEPARTING TRAFFIC SHOULD REMAIN GROUND STOPPED UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE. INBOUND INTERNATIONAL FLIGHTS WILL BE MANAGED ON A CASE BY CASE BASIS.

As of now, the ground stop is through 11:30PM ET, though it’s possible that it’s lifted before then. That timeline clearly reflects the extent to which the current situation is a complete mess, and this won’t be an easy fix.

As usual, JonNYC was among the first to break the news, and he even reported on this before the official ground stop was issued, when airports in the Northeast started having issues, prior to this going nationwide.

Kind of major, started at approx 3:15pmBoston Center, New York Center, Chicago Center, New York Approach have all lost numerous frequencies. All facilities are in ATC Alert. Some sectors in New York Center are unable any traffic currently. Numerous— I mean NUMEROUS frequencies…

“All airspace is currently being sterilized and centers are preparing for ATC Zero operations. Airborne’s should NOT be majorly effected— i.e, at least for now, this is not a “9/11 type of event” where airbornes are being forced to land at the closest airport available. All…

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed this development a while later, sharing that there were “communication issues impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” and he stated that “FAA technicians are investigating the issue.”

The @FAAnews issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them.

As of now, there’s no timeline for this ground stop ending. To my knowledge, I believe this is now the most significant ground stop we’ve seen in the United States in over 25 years (since 9/11).

If you’re flying this weekend, expect that things will be a mess. To those flying right now, good luck. Ford is on a flight that was supposed to depart at 3:59PM, so suffice it to say that he had some pretty bad luck here, as they pushed back, and then this happened. I hope not too many others are in the same situation.

There’s a major issue when you have flights landing but flights can’t depart, since you have way more planes than gates. So get ready to be patient if you’re onboard a flight, given the complicated logistics.

What could explain an air traffic outage of this scale? As of now, all we can do is speculate, though there are a few interesting things to point out.

First, it remains to be seen if this is related, but the FAA reportedly began its rollout of the new AI-powered air traffic management tool this week, known as SMART (which stands for “Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories”).

Timing-wise, it seems like there’s a possibility this could be related. At the same time, you wouldn’t assume this leads to communication issues, which is what seems to be going on here. So it’s worth pointing out the timing, but we have no reason to believe the two things are related.

Yes the FAA began its nationwide rollout of the SMART AI for ARTCCs to use this week. It’s not clear at this time if the rollout is related to this outage, but if it’s a rolling communications issue, it’s much more likely it’s within already established equipment pilots-ATC use https://t.co/PXqSFdOA1q

One can’t help but wonder if a cyber attack might be to blame. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin insists that there are no indications of this being a cyber attack. However, if they’re still investigating the cause, it seems hard to rule anything out.

Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said the agency had no indications of outages being tied to a cyberattack or potential terror threat, adding that the nationwide ground stop was “just a telecommunications outage." https://t.co/cb8xON9Xrz

If this is truly “just a telecommunications outage,” then that represents a major failure. How can air traffic control nationwide have that issue, rather than it just being isolated to one region? Are there no redundancies?

I don’t want to be a conspiracy theorist, but it sure feels to me like some very unusual things are going on. We just saw a huge Microsoft outage, and it has been a very strange week in general. Those two things can of course be completely unrelated, but you can’t help but point it out.

The FAA has grounded flights nationwide, “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” For nearly two hours now, no flights have taken off in the United States, making this the largest outage since 9/11, to my knowledge.

It remains to be seen what the cause of this was, and whether this is a tech glitch, a cyber attack, or what. To those flying now (or this weekend), good luck… you’re going to need it!

What do you make of this strange ATC outage?

#6144. Three Cheers for Gridlock

Democrats are about to get a stern lesson in the separation of powers.

Senator Bernie Sanders (I., Vt.), President Donald Trump, and Senator Elizabeth Warren (D., Mass.)

Alex Wong/Getty Images, Jonathan Ernst, Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters

The ballots from last week’s midterms haven’t even all been counted and congressional Democrats are already all over your money like Jensen Huang on a sexy Chinese spy.

Senator Bernie Sanders wasted no time in renewing his call for Congress to pass Medicare for All, citing various polls showing that the public favors socialized health care dressed up as a modest Medicare expansion. According to a recent White House Council of Economic Advisers estimate, Sanders’s plan would increase federal spending by $32 trillion over the next decade.

Travelers headed to the airport faced the possibility of significant disruptions on Friday evening — and possibly beyond — after an extremely rare nationwide ground stop threatened to upend flight schedules across the United States.

Most departing flights in the U.S.were grounded indefinitely Friday afternoon on orders from the Federal Aviation Administration. The agency cited “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety” in an advisory.

The FAA subsequently attributed the disruption to “communication issues impacting multiple Air Traffic Control Centers” and said FAA technicians were investigating the issue.

Shortly after 5 p.m. EST, the FAA said every flight that was in the air at the time of the ground stop had been accounted for.

“Everybody is safe," U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told reporters. "There is no reason to be concerned about your loved ones if they’re flying, or anything like that."

However, Mullin said the federal government was still working to determine the root cause of the communications outage.

The disruption marked only the second time since 9/11 that a ground stop affecting the entire nation had been issued.

During the last nationwide ground stop in January 2023, more than 10,000 flights were canceled in the fallout of a computer outage at the FAA.

It remains to be seen how significantly flights will be affected this time around. That will largely depend on how long it takes to resolve the issue and for flights to resume.

By 6 p.m. EST, nearly 1,700 U.S. flights scheduled for Friday had been canceled, according to FlightAware. An additional 10,000-plus had been delayed.

That number was likely to grow significantly.

In a statement to TPG, American Airlines said it expected its operations to be affected for the rest of Friday evening.

"It will be all hands on deck across American to get customers on their way as soon as possible when the FAA lifts this ground stop," the carrier said.

Airlines had begun to issue travel advisories. These waivers typically allow passengers with flights booked more flexibility to change their itineraries.

Airlines reported some departures were still permitted as of 6 p.m. EST Friday.

In a social media post, United Airlines said all of its new domestic departures were halted. International departures were being managed on a case-by-case basis, the carrier reported.

Alaska Air Group, which owns Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines, said flights within the state of Alaska were still cleared to operate. Neighbor island service in Hawaii was also unaffected. Departures from the West Coast to Hawaii were also continuing, a spokesperson said.

Typically when a ground stop occurs, flights in the air are permitted to land, but planes on the ground are prohibited from taking off.

Ground stops are frequently issued at individual airports when there is a localized disruption, like bad weather.

But ground stops covering the entire nation have only happened three times this century.

Passengers whose flights are canceled or significantly delayed are entitled to a refund if they choose not to travel or accept a rebooked flight, regardless of the reason for the disruption.

Under Department of Transportation rules, a significant delay generally means arriving at your final destination at least three hours late on a domestic itinerary or six hours late on an international itinerary. Airlines must provide refunds to the original form of payment, not just travel credits, when passengers qualify.

In large-scale travel disruptions like this, rental cars and hotel rooms at or near airports can book up quickly, so it can make sense to act fast if you want to secure a backup option.

If you have airline miles you can use to book a flight for tomorrow, that can also be a good self-insurance policy in case the disruption isn't resolved quickly. Just make sure you understand the cancellation and refund rules before booking a backup ticket.

And while many rewards credit cards offer built-in trip delay or cancellation protection if you used them to book your original airline tickets, it's not guaranteed that those benefits will cover FAA groundings of this nature. Still, save your receipts for any unexpected expenses in case you're eligible for reimbursement.

#6139. “The sitting president doesn’t win”: Ahead of midterms, Trump reflects on himself

On the last day before the 2026 midterm elections, President Donald Trump gave a speech before the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a site of considerable scandal in his second term. He joked it should be renamed after him and spent considerable time discussing Washington, D.C. construction projects and resurrecting conspiracy theories about monument vandals. When the president did turn to the elections, more than 23 minutes into an hour-long speech, he seemed to foreshadow major Republican losses in the House and Senate, describing it as “The most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime.”

“When you vote, remember a party that hates America cannot be allowed to rule over the people who built our country,” Trump said, referring to Democrats, whom he said want to “blow all of this up by electing communist jihadists.”

“If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” Trump said midway in his speech. “Now that doesn’t happen because usually whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, uh, good or bad, good president, great president, bad, for some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot.”

The last day of polling indicates that Democrats have odds that are better than good to flip control of the House and Senate. The final results from the New York Times/Siena University polls report “The party is ahead in all seven states likeliest to decide control of the Senate: Michigan, Kansas, Texas, Maine, Ohio and, more narrowly, Alaska and Iowa.” The final predictions in the Cook Political Report included five additional shifts for Democrats in North Carolina, Florida, Tennessee and Virginia, projecting “that Democrats will win 15 to 25 seats, putting them at a 230- to 240-seat majority.” If a sweep happens in the toss up races, it’ll give Democrats their strongest majority since 2009.

Meanwhile, early voting records have been smashed around the country, in places like South Carolina and Ohio. In Texas, more than 7.7 million voters did so early, surpassing the record turnout for a midterm election set in 2018. Across the nation, about 50 million ballots have already been cast so far, with the share of registered Democrats notably increased in several key state races. But according to the New York Times, around half the expected votes will come on Election Day itself, making it difficult at this point to determine how big a role early votes will play in the outcome.

#6138. Sacha Baron Cohen reveals “Who Is America?” and the answer is terrifying

Showtime debuted Sacha Baron Cohen’s latest series on Sunday, finally providing a partial to the question its title poses. “Who Is America?” The answer, on its face, will not surprise you: we are a nation of easy marks. Not merely easy, but willing.

Baron Cohen bases his career on that knowledge, but watching it in action was much more entertaining two decades ago in the heyday of “Da Ali G Show.” His HBO prank show became a cultural phenomenon before the omnipresence of social media and its accelerated mainstreaming of conspiracy theory as news, before a sitting president began making the denigration of objective journalism into a sport and before the proliferation of junk science as fact.

Back then cameras were not so prevalent as to persuade everyone that they were only one turned corner away from stardom. But today, being on camera is so natural and desirable to most of us that we are willing to say or do just about anything for a few of the 15 minutes we believe to be our birthright.

“Ali G” and the characters the show introduced, including Borat Sagdiyev and Brüno Gehard, also were born years before Project Veritas and InfoWars and other right-wing vehicles of disinformation made hidden camera hoaxing into something sinister.

All of which is to say, “Who Is America?” is not, as Showtime would like you to believe, “the most dangerous show in history.” At best, it is an occasionally funny one.

But to anyone who mourns the collective deterioration of our population’s capacity to engage in critical thought, but has no idea of how urgent of a crisis that happens to be, Baron Cohen’s new endeavor is less of a comedy than a fright show. “Who Is America?” A nation of pliable dullards ripe for the hacking.

“Who Is America?” was produced in secret, and its pre-show marketing largely consisted of publicized declarations of outrage by such right-wing figures as Joe Walsh, Sarah Palin and Roy Moore. Each attempted to transform their extreme embarrassment at having been duped by a British clown hiding behind layers of latex and spirit gum into some approximation of righteous anger at said comedian’s dishonesty.

Showtime, meanwhile, maintained the aura of mystery surrounding the series almost to the brink of its debut, revealing the title only a little more than a week prior. The network released the briefest of clips featuring one famous interview subject, Dick Cheney.

This in itself was a bit of flimflam Showtime’s part: “Hope you’ll tune in next week for an interview with me,” Cheney says in the video, only to be a no-show in the premiere.

You can’t blame “Who Is America?” for saving its biggest fish for later, because the famous politicians in the opener prove the problem of our collective gullibility just fine by themselves. In fact, although liberals may have gotten a hearty guffaw out of hearing Palin’s wailing about having been faked out by Baron Cohen, the very same character — Dr. Billy Wayne Ruddick Jr. PhD of Truthbrary.org — sat down for a conversation with none other than the honorable junior senator from Vermont, Bernie Sanders.

Prior to the premiere Billy Wayne tweeted a response to Palin’s accusation that he made fun disabled veterans. “I did NOT say I was a War Vet,” Ruddick’s “official” response reads, going on to explain that the service was in was “not military, but United Parcel”.

Nor does he make such assertions to Sanders, with whom he debates the merits of a universal healthcare plan. And when I say debate, what I mean is that Sanders very calmly shares statistics with Billy Wayne long after the interviewer’s line of questioning stops making sense. And when Sanders asks Billy Wayne to confirm that he is disabled, given that he is conducting the interview while seated on a motorized scooter, Baron Cohen’s character replies that no, he is not. “This here scooter is to preserve my body’s finite energy,” Billy Wayne says.

READ MORE: That viral “strangers on a plane” Twitter story: Not a rom-com but a horror show

One may be tempted to qualify Sanders’ appearance by pointing out that he acquitted himself well in the face of a person best be described as a few coconuts short of a beach vacation in Binomo.

But this fails to answer the question of why Sanders signed a release, allowing this interview to be broadcast. Did anyone on Sanders’ team vet Truthbrary.org the moment Billy Wayne mentioned it? Even if they thought he was genuine, what is to be gained from being seen in a televised debate with a guy whose site includes a page titled  “Obamanoids — For Real!”?

(To be fair, reportedly Baron Cohen almost fooled veteran news anchor Ted Koppel as part of his project. Koppel told The Hollywood Reporter that he was contacted to appear in a Showtime project titled “Age of Reason,” said to feature “conversations with distinguished experts in science and public policy, highlighting the brightest and most reputable minds on today’s most important topics.” Koppel, perhaps receiving brainwaves from his colleague Sam Donaldson, wised up before Baron Cohen could pull him too deeply into his game.)

A second character introduced in the premiere, an NPR shirt-wearing hyper-liberal named  Nira Cain-N’Degeocello, visits the opulent South Carolina home of wealthy Trump supporters he says are  “afflicted with white privilege.” But it soon becomes clear that his marks’ problem isn’t close-mindedness but over-correcting in the acceptance department. When Baron Cohen’s interviewer waxes on about encouraging his daughter Malala to “free bleed” on the American flag as a lesson, they simply nod and listen; when he chats about his wife’s ongoing affair with a dolphin, they don’t have any questions like, say, whether what they’re hearing is real.

This brings us to another answer to “Who Is America?”: we’re so aware of cameras, and desperate to have its focus upon us, that we will do and say anything without thinking of its possible permanence.

Demonstrating this is Baron Cohen’s third character Rick Sherman, an ex-con turned TV host who visits a Laguna Beach, California gallery to show his work, which is a series of capable but otherwise unextraordinary portraits rendered in feces and ejaculate.

Now, it’s entirely possible that the woman who runs the gallery might have been thinking she could have the next Andres Serrano on her hands. On the other hand, please.

This is a subject entirely aware of being on view, so obsessed with appearing erudite that while Rick is off camera, having excused himself to the facilities to commit another brown-and-white vision to paper, she addresses the camera like the host she was born to be.

“Who knew the world was capable of such oxymoronic paradoxical juxtapositions?” she muses. And this is before the homemade pubic hair paintbrush comes out.

Baron Cohen has pushed the limits of tolerant everyday people many times in the past, mostly in a way that makes them look reasonable or, at the very least, more intelligent than the put-ons he inflicts upon them. And this is perhaps one of the most depressing aspects about “Who Is America?”, its demonstration of how endemic our lack of analysis truly is. I’m not saying that gallery owner is a stupid woman, understand.

But her interview is an example of prizing exposure over lasting consequence. By that I’m not merely referring to the fact that she placated a man who not only handed her pieces of cardboard purportedly smeared with his own dried excrement, or waited to receive a fresh sample of his work, but that she decided she needed to share her expert observation as to why she needed to do so by uttering a sentence full of five dollar words that add up to absolute nonsense.

(Either that or she’s a friend of Baron Cohen’s and in on the gag. I hope it’s option two, as opposed to her actually legitimizing the artistic relevance of number two.)

A number of reviews of “Who Is America?” have pointed out that Baron Cohen’s sneaky deceit is no longer funny because the formerly insane viewpoints Baron Cohen’s tactics expose have been normalized.

This has always been the danger, but it’s one every sort of parody or satire contends with in the current climate. It’s difficult to lampoon leaders seeking to legislate ludicrous patches to crises like gun violence instead of adopting common sense solutions like stricter regulation.

Which brings us to the portion of “Who Is America?” guaranteed to dominate Monday’s gallery of crazy clips, fronted by Baron Cohen’s Col. Erran Morad, a self-styled Israeli anti-terrorism expert who calls himself “the terrorist terminator.”

The fake Mossad officer is there to promote his “Kinderguardians” program, a proposal that aims to train and arm toddlers in the classroom because, Moran says, arming teachers is crazy.

And this is the portion that has Walsh’s boxers in a bunch, because he joins House representatives Dana Rohrabacher and Joe Wilson in lending on-camera endorsements. Walsh’s comments are interwoven with a series of fake testimonials from the likes of Larry Pratt, executive director emeritus of the lobbying group Gun Owners of America and rape joke enthusiast.

Nobody forced Walsh to say, with gusto, “The way to stop a bad guy with is a good child with a gun. Happy shooting, kids!” If he didn’t want to say it, he wouldn’t have.

What Walsh might be upset about is being upstaged by Pratt, who earns some of the episode’s biggest laughs by reading the “science” behind the effectiveness of the fake program, revealing he doesn’t know the difference between human anatomy and hitmakers who grace Billboard’s pop charts.

Yes, “Who Is America?” gets mileage out of highlighting the callousness, sexism and extraordinary gullibility of conservatives, as Baron Cohen always has. But the things they say to him in disguise aren’t all that different than what they’d say on CNN, Fox, MSNBC or talk radio. Whatever power his comedy used to reveal is diminished by the fact that the charlatans no longer operate in secret.

Next week’s episode introduces one or two new characters, although I don’t imagine they do anything more “dangerous” than the four we met on Sunday. For a number of viewers who love Baron Cohen’s schtick, that won’t matter.

To them “Who Is America?” is precisely on brand, showing Americans famous and everyday reacting to bizarre situations with varying degrees of what we consider to be normalcy in a time where the baseline version of normal is constantly morphing and shifting.

To other viewers, however, “Who Is America?” is a confirmation that Baron Cohen has run some tests and can confirm there is limited and ever decreasing brain activity in this worsening patient we know as America. It is something to behold, that’s for sure. But I’m not sure it’s the stuff of groundbreaking comedy. It’s not even really news.
